Question: What is case 1998 CLC 302 about?
Answer: Case 1998 CLC 302 was decided by SUPREME COURT OFAZAD JAMMU KASHMIR on 1997-03-31. The case involved MUHAMMAD HUSSAIN AND OTHERS (APPELLANTS) VERSUS CUSTODIAN OF EVACUEE PROPERTYAND 12 OTHERS RESPONDENTS. The relevant statutes include AZAD JAMMU AND KASHMIR (ADMINISTRATION OF EVACUEE PROPERTY) ACT (II OF 1961 - S. 18-A(1) AZAD JAMMU AND KASHMIR INTERIM CONSTITUTION ACT (VIII OF 1974) - S. 42. The case was heard by SARDAR SAID MUHAMMAD KHAN, C. J. AND MUHAMMAD YUNUS SURAKHVI.

Question: What statutes were applied in case 1998 CLC 302?
Answer: In case 1998 CLC 302, the court applied the following statutes: AZAD JAMMU AND KASHMIR (ADMINISTRATION OF EVACUEE PROPERTY) ACT (II OF 1961 - S. 18-A(1) AZAD JAMMU AND KASHMIR INTERIM CONSTITUTION ACT (VIII OF 1974) - S. 42. This case was heard in SUPREME COURT OFAZAD JAMMU KASHMIR and decided on 1997-03-31.

Question: Who were the lawyers in case 1998 CLC 302?
Answer: The lawyers involved in case 1998 CLC 302 were: ABDUL MAJID MALLICK, ADVOCATE FOR APPELLANTS. CH. SHAH WALI, ADVOCATE FOR RESPONDENTS.. The judges presiding were: SARDAR SAID MUHAMMAD KHAN, C. J. AND MUHAMMAD YUNUS SURAKHVI.

Question: Who were the parties in case 1998 CLC 302?
Answer: The parties in case 1998 CLC 302 were: MUHAMMAD HUSSAIN AND OTHERS (APPELLANTS) VERSUS CUSTODIAN OF EVACUEE PROPERTYAND 12 OTHERS RESPONDENTS. This case was heard in SUPREME COURT OFAZAD JAMMU KASHMIR.

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1998 CLC 302.
Answer: MUHAMMAD YUNUS SURAKHVI, J.-This appeal has been directed against an order passed by the High Court on February 26, 1996, whereby a writ petition filed by the appellants herein was dismissed. 2. The subject of dispute is a land measuring 41 Canals, 17 Marla's, comprises Survey Nos. 10, 11 and 16, situate in village Samantha, Thesis Radial, District Mirror. The disputed land is claimed by the appellants to be in their continuous possession since the time of the ancestors from Dogma Regime. According to the appellants this land was initially allotted to one Adam Shah s/o Muhammad Dm but during the subsistence of the said allotment it was subsequently allotted to one Muhammad Naval, the predecessor-in- interest of respondents 3 to 13 on August 28, 1959. The said allotment was alleged to have been made in favor of allottee in collaboration with the Rehabilitation Authorities. The order of allotment was challenged by the appellants before the D.R.C. but their appeal was dismissed on July 7, 1964. This order of D.R.C. was assailed in revision before the Rehabilitation Commissioner, but it was claimed to be dismissed for want of prosecution in absence of the appellants and the outcome of the same was not conveyed to them. However on October 31, 1991, respondents 3 to 13 secured the provisional proprietary rights transfer order from the Custodian. The appellants challenged the aforesaid order through a review petition before the Custodian of Azad Jammu and Kashmir which was dismissed on October 4, 1994. The aforesaid order of Custodian along with orders of allotment, D.R.C. and the Rehabilitation Commissioner and proprietary rights transfer in favor of appellants were challenged by the appellants by filing a writ petition in the High Court but the same was dismissed vide the order impugned which is the subject of present controversy. 3. It was vehemently contended by Mr. Abdul Maid Wallick, the learned counsel for the appellants, that the impugned order was violative of law and as such label to be set aside. According to the learned counsel the Custodian failed to apply his independent mind to the allotment in question in compliance with the provisions of law as the appellants were admittedly old tenants in the land in dispute as such the failure on the part of the learned Custodian to examine the allotment in the light of sections 18-A(1) and 18-B of the Amended Administration of the Evacuee Property Act was tantamount to failure of exercise of jurisdiction. According to the learned counsel it was wrong to suggest that the points raised before the learned Custodian and the High Court were purely questions of fact needing detailed inquiry, as such not within the purview of High Court in exercise of its writ jurisdiction. The learned counsel -posted out that the learned Judge in the High Court failed to examine the copies of record of rights appended with the writ petition showing that the appellants were the old tenants in the land as they continuously occupied the same since the Dogma Regime through their ancestors. It also escaped the attention of the learned Judge in the High Court that the status of appellants as old tenants was admitted by respondents in their written statement. Thus, according to the learned counsel the Custodian and the learned Judge in the High Court misdirected themselves in not attending to the point of determining the status of appellants as old tenants and its effect on the allotment in question. 4. In reply, it was contended by Ch. Shah Walk, the learned counsel representing the respondents that finding of facts finally concluded by the Rehabilitation Authorities on the basis of material placed before them were open to no exception by challenging the same through a constitutional petition The learned counsel submitted that the proprietary rights transfer order was passed in favor of respondents on the basis of valid allotment as such the review petition before the Custodian did not merit any consideration. According to the learned counsel the matter was finally determined by the Rehabilitation Authorities on all forums who were vested with the jurisdiction to determine the same and the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere in the findings arrived at by the competent authorities. The learned counsel maintained that the appellants never applied for the allotment of the land till the same was August m favor of allottee and all the proceedings initiated for its cancellation ended, upholding the allotment of the allottee as genuine. According to the learned counsel for respondents the claim of appellants as being old tenants was also disallowed by the Rehabilitation Authorities. 5. After harem the respective contentions of the learned counsel for the parties and going through the record, it may be stated that the land in dispute was admittedly allotted in favor of Muhammad Naval, the predecessor-MN-interest of respondents 3 to 13 on August 28, 1959. This order was challenged by way of appeal but the same was dismissed by D.R.C. on July 7, 1964. Revision petition filed before the Rehabilitation Commissioner against the order of D.R.C. was also dismissed on February 25, 1967. On the basis of entitlement certificate issued by the Rehabilitation Commissioner the provisional proprietary rights transfer order was issued on October 31, 1991, which was challenged through a review petition before the Custodian, but it was disallowed vide order, dated October 4, 1994. It is pertinent to post out that at the time of challenging the allotment order it was categorically averred by the appellants that they were the old tenants and the land in question was in their continuous possession since Dogma Regime. In the alternative it was also averred that land be allotted to the appellants. The question of allotment in favor of respondents was concurrently resolved by the Rehabilitation Authorities on all the forums to be genuine, and it was also opined that the appellants in presence of allotment in favor of respondents were not entitled to the allotment of the land in dispute. Nevertheless the fact remains that none of the Rehabilitation Authorities determine the question of status of appellants in the land in question as old tenants. The D.R.C. formed the view that since the plea of appellants being old tenants was not raised before Tonsilar Custodian, so the same could not be raised before him. It 1s, however, an underlying fact that post was raised before D.R.C. Rehabilitation Commissioner, the Custodian and then before the High Court but all of them failed to advert to the above post. Instead all of them adverted only to the point that allotment in favor of respondents had attained finality as the same was conclusively determined by the Rehabilitation Authorities. We also concur with the aforesaid view that the allotment in favor of respondents indeed attained the finality as none of the Rehabilitation Authorities was persuaded to annul the same. But we may observe that the question with regard to the status of appellants as being old tenants in the land in question, as said earlier, was, though raised, specifically, but not resolved which has resulted into miscarriage of justice. The first proviso of section 18-A(1) 01 Administration of Evacuee Property Act as amended in Azad Jammu and Kashmir on January 14, 1987, under No.19–123/LD/LEG(A)/1987 reads as under:- "Provided that in the case where the Evacuee Property is held by any old tenant as defined in Government Order, then, notwithstanding the grant of proprietary rights to the allottees in respect of such Evacuee Property, the old tenant shall have the protection against the ejectment to the extent indicated in para. 1(e) of the Government Order No. and he shall be label to pay the rent to the allottee as provided therein." The above provision shows that an old tenant shall have the protection against the ejectment to the extent of land provided in the Government Order No. para. 1(e). For the sake of convenience para. 1(e) of Government Order is reproduced below: 'Old tenant! would mean such tenants as are recorded to have been tenants of evacuee property immediately before the War of Liberation started: Provided that the total land in possession of such tenants m whatever capacity does not exceed 24 Canals in all: Provided further, that the land shall be allotted to the refugees and the tenants shall be liable to pay the same rent to the allottees as they paid to. the evacuee landowners." w The above-referred'’ provision of law makes it abundantly clear that while granting proprietary rights to the allottees it was also enjoyed upon the Custodian to resolve the question of status of appellants in the land in question as old tenants and to protect their rights at the time of ejectment to the extent provided in the relevant law. But the learned Custodian has adverted to the point of status of the appellants as old tenants as under: I The question as to whether the appellants enjoy the status of old tenants and are entitled to enjoy the protection under Order were not resolved at all. 6. Even a question of fact which could have been determined on the basis of perusal of record without adverting to making a detailed enquiry is permissible under law to be resolved in exercise of writ jurisdiction. In the instant case the status of appellants being old tenants MN the land in question is admitted by the respondents in their written statement as they did not repudiate the said assertion rather it was alleged that the appellants failed to pay the share of the produce of the land to the evacuee owners. Besides* there was a bulk of evidence existing on the record which purports to show that the land in question was in continuous possession of the appellants SME Dogma Regime. In Jacaranda 1957-1958 B.K. the forefathers of the appellants are shown in the possession of the land in question on payment of fixed revenue. In Jacaranda 1992-1993 B.K. Muhammad Hussain, one of the appellants and Abdul Rehman and Muhammad Nawab the ancestors of appellants, are shown in possession of the land in question on the payment of share of produce. In Jacaranda 2000-2001 B.K. Muhammad Baths, the ancestor of appellants, is entered in the possession of the land on the payment of share of produce. In Jacarandas 1957-1958, 1981-1982 A.D. the appellants are entered in possession of the land on payment of fixed revenue in some portion of it and share of produce in the other portion of the land. Thus, there remains no manner of doubt that the land in question is shown in continuous possession of the appellants since the time of their ancestors from Dogma Regime up to the present time and the learned D.R.C. Rehabilitation Commissioner, Custodian and the High Court failed to determine the status of appellants as being old tenants which could have been very easily determined on perusal of the relevant record available. We, therefore, have no hesitation to hold that the appellants are old tenants in the land in question and their status as such remains undisputed by the respondents. 7. In the review petition before the Custodian it has been specifically alleged in the memo, of review petition by the appellants that they belong to three different families, but their total holding is only 44 Canals. However, the learned Custodian in his judgment in the review petition has mentioned that the counsel for the appellant argued before him that their holding measures 34 Canals. The question whether they belong to one family or three families and whether their other holding measures 44 Canals or 34 Canals have not been adverted to at all. During the course of arguments the learned counsel for the appellants contended that lit of 24 Canals under Government Order, per family has been changed through an amendment. While consider mg the question of benefit to the appellants as old tenants all these questions are relevant and need resolution. The learned Custodian has expressed the view that as there was nothing on the record to show that the appellants-tenants paid any rent to evacuee-Hindus, they are not entitled to the benefit envisaged under Order. The aforesaid observation of the Custodian is contradictory to his observation that question of benefit of Government Order may be raised and resolved at the time when the appellants are ejected. Even otherwise, the observation is also unsustainable because no such objection appears to have been taken by the respondents at any stage previously nor the same was resolved. Thus there being no finding whether the appellants are entitled to benefit under Order, the question of application of res judicata does not arise. 8. In light of what has been stated above, we partly accept the appeal, set aside the impugned orders of the Custodian and the High Court. The case is remanded to the Custodian with the direction to inquire into the matter whether the appellants are entitled to take the benefit of Order and if so to what extent. The Custodian while dealing with the matter may strike issues in the light of above observations and decide the question of protection to the appellants under Order according to law. Before parting with the case we may observe that under the first proviso of section 18-A(1) of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, it is desirable that the question of protection to an old tenant, if raised before Custodian is decided at the time of issuing of Proprietary Rights Transfer Order. The appeal is accepted as indicated above. Appeal partly accepted.

Question: What is case 1998 MLD 1020 about?
Answer: Case 1998 MLD 1020 was decided by GILGIT CHIEF COURT on 1997-10-17. The case involved THE ST ATE (PETITIONER) VERSUS SHAHZAD WALI AND OTHERS (RESPONDENTS). The relevant statutes include CRIMINAL PROCEDURE CODE (V OF 1898) - S. 497(5) PENAL CODE (XLV OF 1860) - SS. 302/324/307/34 AND 392 OFFENCES AGAINST PROPERTY (ENFORCEMENT OF HUDOOD) ORDINANCE (VI OF 1979) - S. 17 WEST PAKISTAN ARMS ORDINANCE (XX OF 1965) - S. 13. Question: Who were the parties in case 1998 MLD 1020?
Answer: The parties in case 1998 MLD 1020 were: THE ST ATE (PETITIONER) VERSUS SHAHZAD WALI AND OTHERS (RESPONDENTS). This case was heard in GILGIT CHIEF COURT.

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1998 MLD 1020.
Answer: WW. 1. This single Order will dispose of the abovementioned two applications for cancellation of bail, as both of them arise out of one and the same F.LR. 2. According to the report lodged by Rashid Iqbal son of Mir Haman, resident of Kumar Band, This and District Abbottabad, the prosecution story runs thus:-- That the maker of the report on 15-10-1996 at 12-10 p.m. went to the Police Station Gil git and lodged a report before Station House Officer to the effect that he is a cleaner of Truck No.GITA- 2937 and while Abdul Attar resident of Abbottabad was the driver of the Truck in question; that on 14-10-1996 at Most situate within the limits of Huzza, one Saved resident of Benji engaged their truck from Most to Gil git for Rs.5,500 and his goods were loaded in the truck and at about 5 p.m. after loading the goods, they started for Gil git and at about 9 p.m. when they crossed the Check Post at Danish, a car of black color which had a revolving light on its roof, overtook the truck and proceeded ahead, while the Driver Abdul Attar stopped the truck at Petrol Pump Aliased, in order to fill the diesel in the truck and thereafter they proceeded towards Gil git; that at about 12.30 a.m. when they covered a distance of 13 k.m. ahead of Sikandarabad towards Gil git, the aforesaid car once again came from behind and crossed the truck and after covering a little distance, the car was stopped on the road in a slanting position and the revolving light on the roof of the car was on; that the driver and the cleaner took it to be a police car and therefore stopped the truck; that from the said car some unknown persons who were armed with automatic weapons started firm, as a result of which Abdul Attar driver received bullet juries on his head and chest, while the cleaner also sustained fire-arm injuries on his arm and other parts of the body, when the driver was hit, the truck became out of control, and it collided against the said very car, from which the unknown culprits had fired shots at them; that Abdul Attar breathed his lost in the truck, while the cleaner in injured condition ran back and after covering some distance, he climbed a mountain and spent the night in a cave and at dawn he came down to the road and found that both the truck and dead body of the driver were missing; that Rashid Iqbal in injured condition left for Gil git in a car, which was proceeding towards. Gil git, in order to make a report at the Police Station. On his arrival at Police Station Gil git, Rashid Iqbal reported the matter to Syed Burk Shah, S.H.O. who recorded his report and registered a case under section / /341, P.P.C. read with section 17 of the Barnabas Offenses Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979, vide F.I.R. No.254 of 1996. WW. Thereafter, the Investigating Agency came in motion. Burk Shah, S.H.O. handed over the investigation to Fatal Ahmad S.I.P. who left for the spot. Rashid Iqbal in injured condition was sent to District Headquarter Hospital Gil git for medical examination and treatment and his blood-stained clothes were also taken into possession by the police. '. Fatal Ahmad S.I.P. on his arrival at the scene of occurrence, recovered Identity Card of Abdul Attar driver (deceased) from his pocket along with Rs.6,224 and one blood-stained pocket-diary was also taken into possession in the presence of Larger and Attar- Rehman, marginal witnesses. The Investigating Officer collected 20 empty shells of 7.62 M.M. rifle, four pieces of mudguard of the damaged car, three pieces of mirror light and the pieces of -brake-light of the said car were also taken into possession from the scene of occurrence by the very Investigating Officer Fatal Ahmad,' in the presence of Baba Khan and Ghulam Mehdi, marginal witnesses. Mr. Haviour Rehman, District Attorney representing the State and Malik Had Nawab, Counsel for the accused/respondents were heard at length and record of the case was perused with their able assistance. j- 6. The learned District Attorney put a lot of stress during the course of his arguments that the Sessions Judge has passed an illegal order by allowing bail to the accused/respondents. He argued that no doubt, section /307, P.P.C. are compoundable and the legal heirs of the deceased Abdul Attar driver have compromised the murder case by receiving three lac rupees from the accused party and the impugned order is valid up to that extent, but so far section 392, P.P.C. and section 17 Barnabas are concerned, these sections are not compoundable and fall under the prohibitory clause of section 497, Cr.P.C. He further stated that when a Dacoity takes place on a highway and during the transaction a murder takes place then the offense falls under section 17(4), Barnabas Offenses Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979, which reads as under:- M (4) Whoever, being an adult, is guilty of Barnabas in the course of which. he commits murder shall be punished with death imposed as Had. 7. The learned District Attorney also stated that in the case in hand, all the three accused are adults, and they have committed dacoity on the highway by kill mg Abdul Attar driver and injuring Rashid Iqbal cleaner of the truck by firing at them with their automatic weapons from the black car belonging, to Shaheed Walk accused and the Sessions Judge was not legally correct by incorporating in his impugned order that punishment for Barnabas is 14 years with whipping not exceeding thirty stripes and the impugned order is altogether liable to be set aside. 8. On the other hand, Malik Had Nawab, Advocate appearing on behalf of the. accused/respondents argued that section /307, P.P.C. are compoundable, and the matter has been patched up between the legal heirs of the deceased Abdul Star and accused party, who paid three lac rupees as "Diet" to the legal heirs of the deceased and referred to the statements of MST. Sabina Bibi widow of Abdul Attar deceased and Vardar Muhammad brother of the deceased as well as the statement of Rashid Iqbal, cleaner of the WW. truck who had sustained bullet injuries on different parts of his body during the dacoity on the highway. ' 9. When the learned Counsel for the accused/respondents was asked whether section 392, P.P.C. and section 17(4) of the Barnabas Offenses Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979 are compoundable or not. He frankly conceded and rightly to that when a dacoity is committed on the highway by an adult person and during the course of which, he commits murder shall be punished with death imposed as Had. 10. From the bare reading of section 17(4) of the Barnabas Offenses Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979, it is crystal clear that, whoever, being an adult, is guilty of Barnabas in the course of which he commits murder shall be punished with death as Had, the Sessions Judge Gil git has not applied his mind regarding this section of law. 11. Keep mg ITO consideration the circumstantial evidence, in the shape of recoveries as mentioned above, coupled with the exculpatory confessional X statement of accused Sherman recorded under section 164, CRP.C. by Muhammad Abbas, Assistant Commissioner/MIC Gil git on 29-10-1996, prima facie, the accused/respondents are linked with the offenses under section 392 P.P.C, and section 17(4) of the Barnabas Offfenc.es Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979, which are not compoundable and the punishment for Barnabas is the forfeiture of life as Had, which falls within the prohibitory clause of section 497, Cr.P.C. the accused/respondents are not entitled to bail. The result is that I recall the impugned orders and the accused/respondents present in Court on bail, are taken into custody and remanded to judicial lock-up as under trial prisoners. 12. Before parting with the judgment, it is disquieting to note that Sessions Judge Gil git has passed the impugned order without applying his mind to section 392, P.P.C. read with section 17(4) of the Hara bah Offenses Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979, which are not compoundable and fall under the prohibitory clause of section 497, Cr.P.C. but on the other hand, Mr. Ghana Sessions Judge Gil git kept his eyes shut to this aspect of the case that in a dacoity case on the highway, when murder takes place, the punishment imposed is death as Had, while going through the order, one can get the impression that Mr. Ghana was under great pressure, political or local which compelled him to accept the bail application by releasing all the three accused/respondents WW. on bail and this action on his part naturally tells upon his integrity. Moreover, it affects adversely the image of the judiciary in eyes of public. 13. Copies of this order be circulated among all the Sessions Judges and Judicial Magistrates for their future guidance. 14. The ma'am case under section / /341, P.P.C. and section 17 of the Barnabas Offenses Against Property (Enforcement of Hudson) Ordinance, 1979 read with section 13(B) No.20 of Arms Ordinance 1965 stands transferred from the Court of Mr. Mahmood Ghana, Sessions Judge Gil git to the Court of Mr. Muhammad Ali, Sessions Judge Diaper for disposal, with the direction that he should try the case at Gil git as and when he happens to be on tour to Gil git. Bail cancelled

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1998 MLD 997.
Answer: k m To begin with, on 8-1-1997 Ghulam Hussein, Station House Officer was busy in the investigation of a case under section, Offense Against Property (Enforcement of WW. Hudson) Ordinance 1979 read with section 457 P.P.C. registered vide F.I.R. No. 11 of 1996, the. accused/respondents Broader Aman and Sultan Adam, residents of Tangier Koran gay, District Diaper, who were suspected, informed the S.H.O. that they have no hand in the burglary case for which they are beg interrogated, but they disclosed to the very Investigating Officer that they are trafficking m arms and contraband OMM, and they further apprised the Investigating Officer that they had brought some opium and one China made pistol for selling to Monza Under and were in search of a customer; that they could not find any customer there, and therefore they concealed the contraband OMM and the unlicenced pistol at village Under near Burbot Bridge on the bank of river and themselves proceeded towards Gin day in search of a customer, when they were arrested by the local police. 2. Armed with this formation, Ghulam Hussain S.H.O. in the company of A.S.I. Muhammad Diaz, Reheat Being H.C. Baba Khan and FIDA Muhammad Shah constables left for Monza Under along with the accused/respondents who were mm custody of the police and across the river, near Burbot Bridge from the bank of the river, at the instance and plantation of accused/respondent Broader Aman, in the presence of Numbardar Mag sad Ali Khan, Boo Jan, GUL Ghana, Fair Muhammad and Malik Muhammad, residents of village Under, from underneath, two big stones a bag of white color was recovered and on opening the same, the Investigating Officer found two plastic pieces. In one plastic, 30 bore pistol made in China, one spare magazine besides live rounds of 30 bore pistol and in other piece of plastic', contraband opium was found, and the opium was weighed in the nearby shop of one Mira Ali Khan in the presence of the aforesaid marginal witnesses. On weighing the contraband opium, the total quantity was found 3750 grams and the opium was sealed into a parcel. ] 3. On the basis of the recovery of contraband opium and the unlicenced 30 bore pistol along with live rounds of 30 bore pistol etc. the Investigating Officer registered a case against the accused/respondents Broader Aman and Sultan Adam. 4. The accused/respondents approached the Sessions Judge Guitar for bail, who in his tum after hearing the arguments, pro and contra, enlarged the accused/respondents on bail, subject to their furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs.50,000 WW. with two sureties each, in the like amount to the satisfaction of S.D.M. Penial, vide his order dated 6-3-1997. 5. Feeling dissatisfied with the impugned order, passed by the Sessions Judge Guitar, the State moved the present application for cancellation of bail granted to the accused/respondents. 6. I have heard Mr. Haviour Rehman, District Attorney on behalf of the State and Malik Had Nawab, Advocate for the accused/respondents and also studied the file. 7. The accused/respondents while in custody m another case, admitted before the S.H.O. Ghulam Hussain that they are innocent so far the theft is concerned, and they farther informed the Investigating Officer that they are dealing in contraband opium and arms; that they had come to village Under in search of a customer in order to sell contraband OPM and one unlicenced pistol, but they could not get any customer, therefore, they started for village Gin day and have concealed the opium and the unlicenced 30 bore pistol across the river near Burbot Bridge on the bank of the river. The accused/respondents while in handcuffs led the police to the bridge in question and from near the bridge on the bank of the river, at the instance and rotation of Broader Aman, accused/respondent, recovered one China Made 30 bore pistol, one spare magazine along with live rounds of 30 bore pistol and 3750 grams of contraband opium duly wrapped in different plastic pieces, in the presence of the marginal witnesses. The offense of dealing in contraband OMM falls under the prohibitory clause of section 497, Cr.P.C. as the punishment provided for the same is imprisonment for life. 8. For the aforesaid reasons, the Sessions Judge Guitar was not justified to allow bail to the accused/respondents. I, therefore, recall the impugned order and cancel the bail granted to the accused/respondents. The accused/respondents present in Court are to be taken into custody and remanded to judicial lock-up as under trial prisoners. Bail cancelled. WW.

Question: Who were the lawyers in case 1955 PLD 2?

Question: Who were the parties in case 1955 PLD 2?
Answer: The parties in case 1955 PLD 2 were: CUSTODIAN OF EVACUEE PROPERTY, PUNJAB W. GOPAL DAS AND MRS. GOPAL DAS (PETITIONERS) VERSUS REHABILITATION AUTHORITY (RESPONDENT). This case was heard in CUSTODIAN (PB.).

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1955 PLD 2.
Answer: A. M. Jan, (Custodian)-(8th December, 1954).-The petitioners Mr. and Mrs. Goal Was made an application to the Deputy Custodian Lahore, under section 17, Evacuee Property Ordinance, for a certificate that the property which they whish to sell is not evacuee property. Or the property of tending evacuees and that the proposed sale may be. sanctioned. The Deputy Custodian recorded the statement of Mr. Goal Was and declined to give the certificate asked for on the ground that the petitioners are either evacuees or intending evacuees. This is a vague finding. The term “evacuee” has been clearly defined and if the petitioners came within the purview of that definition they should have been declared evacuees. The term “intending evacuee” includes any person against whom an intention to settle in the territories now comprising India or in any area occupied by India is established from his conduct or form documentary evidence. The learned Deputy Custodian has relied upon this Provision of law, contained in section 2 (3-A), Evacuee Property Ordinance. He should, therefore, have said that the petitioners were, MN his opinion, intending evacuees. But, for declaring people as intending evacuees the procedure laid down in section 23-A Evacuee Property Ordinance, must be followed 1-e. where the Custodian, or the A Deputy Custodian, has reason to believe that, a person is an intending evacuee he should give notice to such person and call upon him to show cause why he should not be declared an intending evacuee. After holding such inquiry into the matter as the circumstances of the case require an order should be passed, stat mg the reasons therefor, declaring such person to be an intending evacuee or not; and any declaration so made must be published in the official Gazette. No notice was given to the petitioners to show cause why they should not be declared intending evacuees and the case must be heard de novo in accordance with law. As the learned Deputy Custodian Lahore has expressed his opinion in the matter it would not be right to send the case back to him for re-adjudication. I, therefore, send it to the Deputy Custodian (General) who will give proper notice to the petitioners under section 23-A and then decide whether they are intending evacuees or not. From the order of the Deputy Custodian (General) the petitioners will have the might of appeal to me under section 36, Evacuee Property Ordinance. A. h. Order accordingly.

The relevant statutes include CUSTODIAN PAKISTAN (ADMINISTRATION OF EVACUEE PROPERTY) ORDINANCE (XV OF 1949) -S, 23. The case was heard by CONSTANTINE, C. J, AND MUNSHI.

Question: What statutes were applied in case 1955 PLD 265?
Answer: In case 1955 PLD 265, the court applied the following statutes: CUSTODIAN PAKISTAN (ADMINISTRATION OF EVACUEE PROPERTY) ORDINANCE (XV OF 1949) -S, 23. This case was heard in SINDH HIGH COURT and decided on 1954-09-24.

Question: Who were the lawyers in case 1955 PLD 265?
Answer: The lawyers involved in case 1955 PLD 265 were: DINGOMALN. FOR PETITIONER. NASIR SHAHMIR FOR RESPONDENTS.. The judges presiding were: CONSTANTINE, C. J, AND MUNSHI.

Question: Who were the parties in case 1955 PLD 265?
Answer: The parties in case 1955 PLD 265 were: BHAGWANDAS MOTUMAL—PETITIONER VERSUS CUSTODIAN OF EVACUEE PROPERTYAND ANOTHER — RESPONDENTS. This case was heard in SINDH HIGH COURT.

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1955 PLD 265.
Answer: [This was a writ petition to quash the order of the Deputy Custodian, Sukkur, that certain buildings and the confectionery known as M. B. Anagram Factory installed in them, including machinery etc. was evacuee property to the extent of 0-15-0 share, belonging to an evacuee Hassan and. The petitioner later abandoned his claim m regard to a parcel of the buildings. After setting out fully the course of the litigation, between the petitioner and the evacuee, before the Deputy, Assistant and Additional Custodians and the Custodian, the judgment proceeded:] Constantine, C. J—We are therefore left with the order of the Deputy Custodian as the only order relating to the confectionery business, and Mr. Diagonal contends that this order has been passed without any evidence. We have summarized the judgment of the Deputy Custodian, and it will be seen that evidence on the part of Hassan and consisted of letters written by Hassan and, letters of the Income-tax Officer and of the City Survey Officer. No proof of these letters was called. The facts stated in these letters were facts which were to be proved by oral evidence. Thus the provisions of section 60 of the Evidence Act were contravened. The Evidence Act by section provides that it applies to all judicial proceedings in or before any Court. The definition of Court m section 3 is that unless a contrary intention appears from the context, Court includes all Judges and Magistrates and all persons, except arbitrators, legally authorized to take evidence. It is common ground that the Deputy Custodian was conducting an inquiry, Mr. Nasir argues that these proceeding - were only quasi-judicial. We do not think that these proceedings were merely quasi-judicial proceedings. Section 23 states that when holding an inquiry, the Custodian shall have the same powers as are vested in a Court under the Code of Civil Procedure when trying a suit in respect of enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him on oath or affirmation, compelling the discovery and production of documents, articles and things, issuing a commission for the examination of witnesses, and any prescribed matter. Moreover for the purposes of section 196 and within the meaning of sections 193 and 228, every proceeding shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding. Furthermore, in rule 11 framed under section 47 (1) is stated that the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure shall, as far as possible and subject to such modification as the Custodian may direct, to follow. We have therefore, no doubt that the proceedings before a Custodian when he is conducting an inquiry under the Act, as opposed to B an administration matter, are judicial. It maybe also posted that the Custodian’s Department itself recognizes the difference between the judicial functions of the Custodian and its administrative functions since certain officials are designated as judicial. Nowhere in the Deputy Custodian’s judgment is there stated to be any admission on the part of Bhagwan or his witnesses that the alleged transaction related to not only the building, but to the confectionary business as well. The sale-deed of 1944 mentioned no machinery except “an electric meter and electricity which were closed.” The Kabuhayat of 1945 mention meter and electric fittings.” The receipt states “and machmerywala”. The application under section 18 was headed “and Machinery” and that the word “machinery” was mentioned in the first paragraph. That is all. We can find therefore nothing which can be construed as an admission that the contents of the buildings ever belonged at all to Hassan and. We think, therefore, that the Deputy Custodian’s order declaring the confectionery factory evacuee property, was passed without any evidence, and we consider that such an order was contrary to the principles of natural justice. The order ordering possession to be taken of not only Suit Nos. 784 1-A and B, but also possession of the machinery in those buildings which was passed, being founded upon the judicial order of the Deputy Custodian, is unsupported in so far as it relates to the machinery (except the meter and electric fittings) and other movables constituting the confectionary factory. As regards build mg 784 2-A and 2-B, Mr. Nasir was uncertain whether possession of buildings had been taken in fact or not, and conceded that if possession had been taken, it had been wrongly taken. The order, therefore, will be that the order of the Deputy Custodian E. F. Sukkur in application No. dated 28th August 1952 in so far as it states that the 0-15-0 Anna share in the confectionery machinery installed therein belongs to respondent Hassan and is evacuee property, is quashed; The possession of the build mg 784 2-A and 2-B and the machinery therein, if taken, is illegal. A. h. Order quashed.

Question: What is case 1955 PLD 10 about?
Answer: Case 1955 PLD 10 was decided by CUSTODIAN (PB.) on 1955-04-15. The case involved CUSTODIAN OF EVACUEE PROPERTY PROGRESSIVE PAPERS LID. LAHORE VERSUS THE REHABILITATION AUTHORITY, PUNJAB. The relevant statutes include PAKISTAN (ADMINISTRATION OF EVACUEE PROPERTY) ORDINANCE (XV OF 1949) - SS. 15 AND 16. The case was heard by A. M. JAN.

Question: What statutes were applied in case 1955 PLD 10?
Answer: In case 1955 PLD 10, the court applied the following statutes: PAKISTAN (ADMINISTRATION OF EVACUEE PROPERTY) ORDINANCE (XV OF 1949) - SS. 15 AND 16. This case was heard in CUSTODIAN (PB.) and decided on 1955-04-15.

Question: Who were the lawyers in case 1955 PLD 10?
Answer: The lawyers involved in case 1955 PLD 10 were: MAHMOOD ALL QASURI, FOR THE PETITIONER. SAEED-UD-DIN, R. O. LEGAL, FOR THE R. A.. The judges presiding were: A. M. JAN.

Question: Who were the parties in case 1955 PLD 10?
Answer: The parties in case 1955 PLD 10 were: CUSTODIAN OF EVACUEE PROPERTY PROGRESSIVE PAPERS LID. LAHORE VERSUS THE REHABILITATION AUTHORITY, PUNJAB. This case was heard in CUSTODIAN (PB.).

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1955 PLD 10.
Answer: A. M. Jan, (Custodian).-This order will be read in continuation of my order dated 24th July, 1954, whereby I sent the case to the Deputy Custodian (General) for taking evidence on the points mentioned in that order. The evidence recorded by the Deputy Custodian WW. (General) is of eight witnesses, P. W. 1, Malik Anwar Khan, Associate of Indian Institute of Architects, has given the rates of second class buildings and characterized the building of the Tribune Press as a 2nd class public building. P. W. 2, Abdul Aziz Khan, Architectural Engineer gave the area occupied by the building and the value of the land adjacent to it. P. W. 3, Abdul Rashid, Proprietor, Lion Press, Lahore, gave a description of the machinery and its market value. P. W. 4, Syed Amir Hussain Shah, Managing Director Progressive Papers Ltd. stated the facts relating to the agreement to sell, the details of the amount paid by them to the Government, its various Departments, the Lahore Corporation and some third party claims. The total amount comes to Rs. 1,27,755-11-6. P. W. 5, Main Eftekhari- adding gave a history of the negotiations resulting in the agreement to sell the property. He also deposed that the machinery the Progressive Papers Limited purchased from the Tribune Trust was worthless, and he had to go to America for buying new machinery which cost about Rs. 10,00,000. P. W. 6, Misti Oahu- adding says that if he had to purchase the machinery installed in the Tribune Press, he would not have paid more than for scrap iron. P. W. 7, Diaz Ahmad, owner of It Press, Lahore, said that the machinery in the Tribune Press was old and worn out. P. W. 8, Hammed Allah made a statement to the same effect.- The evidence of Syed Amir Hussain Shah, M. L. A. Managing Director, Progressive Papers Limited, which, has not been challenged, proves that Rs. 1,26,085-13-6 has been paid by them to the Government and other local bodies. The rest of the evidence shows that the price agreed upon was adequate consideration. Counsel for the petitioners tendered in evidence the file of case No. 39 of 1949. The documentary evidence on this file shows that the Trustees of the Tribune Press had agreed to sell the property in question to the petitioners and by their resolution dated 10th June 1949, they empowered Rai Broader Bari Days to execute a special power of attorney in favor of Mr. Sharma and Mr. Bali authorizing them to execute and register the sale deed in favor of the petitioners. The Trustees had at that time left Pakistan on account of the setting up of the two dominions of Pakistan and India, or on account of civil disturbances or the fear of such disturbances. They were unable to personally occupy, supervise or manage the Trust property, and it was not occupied, supervised or managed by anyone whose authority to do so had been approved by the Custodian. It had, therefore, become evacuee property which has been defined to mean any property in which an. evacuee has any right or interest whether personally or as a trustee or a beneficiary or in any other capacity. According to para 20 of Vardar Deal Singh’s Will, dated the 15th June, 1895, the property WW. pertaining to the Tribune Press was to vest in the Trustees thereof: After the partition, when the Trustees went away from Pakistan and became evacuees their property became vested in the Custodian under section 6 of the Evacuee Property Ordinance (XV of 1949) The Progressive Papers Limited have, therefore, applied to the Custodian for the confirmation of the agreement made by the Trustees. According to section 6, para. 2, of the Evacuee Property Ordinance any evacuee property which is held in Trust for religious or charitable purposes shall remain vested in the Custodian only till such time as fresh trustees are apported in the manner provided by Law and pending the appointment of fresh trustees the Trust property and the income thereof shall be applied by the Custodian for fulfilling as far as possible, the purposes of the Trust. The question arises whether the Custodian can, during the time when he is in charge of the property, sell the property or he can merely use it for the -purposes of the Trust. Counsel for the petitioners says that in this case the property is already under an agreement of sale made by the Trustees and the Custodian is asked merely to give his approval to that contract. This gives rise to the next question whether, the Trustees had, after they had become evacuees, any power to make a contract in respect of this property. The answer to this question is that there was nothing to prevent them from making a contract, but the contract cannot be enforced without the permission of the Custodian. Section 15 of the Evacuee Property Ordinance prohibits the transfer of property, in areas relating to which a Notification has been issued, except with the previous approval in writing of the Custodian. If the Custodian gives his approval to the completion of this contract, the Trustees have the power to complete the sale ; otherwise not. Section 16 says that no creation or transfer of any right or merest in or encumbrance upon any property made in any manner whatsoever, on or after the first day of March, 1947, by or on behalf of any evacuee or by or on behalf of a person \Who has or may hereafter become an evacuee after the date of such creation or transfer shall be effective so as to confer any right or remedy on any party thereto or on any person claiming under any such party, unless it is confirmed by the Custodian. This section relates to transfers or creation of merest effected without the previous approval of the Custodian and here too what is required to regularize the transfer, or the creation of interest, is the approval of the Custodian. Section 17 says that where any transfer has been made, or any interest has been created by virtue of a document, without the approval of the Custodian under section 16, the document will not be registered unless the party presenting it produces a certificate from the Custodian showing that the property is not evacuee property, or that the transaction has been confirmed by the Custodian. The only question that remains, therefore, is whether the WW. Custodian should give his approval to this agreement for sale and allow the sale to be completed and registered. There is no reason to suppose that it was not a bona fide transaction or that the consideration was not adequate. The condition imposed by the Notification of the Central Government regarding the payment of consideration appears to have been complied with. The Central Government and the Rehabilitation Authority have no objection to the grant of approval for the completion of the sale. Last month received letter No. 1366-Reh-IV/55, dated the 8th March, 1955 from the Rehabilitation Commissioner and the Secretary to the Government, Punjab, saying that the Central Government had in their letter dated 20th May, 1954 asked the Custodian to examine the case in the light of their Notification dated 10th April, 1954 and, if it was found that the case was eligible for completion, it should be allowed to be completed. It was also said that in an earlier communication, dated 22nd December 1948, the Custodian was advised by the Hon’BLE Minister for Refugees that permission might be given to the Progressive Papers Limited to purchase this property and to treat it as a special case and that lately the Central Minister for Refugees and Rehabilitation had expressed anxiety! for the confirmation of this sale on the ground that the requirements of the Notification above-mentioned had been duly fulfilled. In view of these facts the Secretary, to Government, Punjab, Rehabilitation Department wrote that the Counsel for the Rehabilitation Department was being instructed to withdraw from the case and that the case should be decided by me in accordance with the provisions of Law. I directed the R. O. (Legal) to remain in attendance and assist the Court in deciding the case according to the provisions of Law. Counsel for the petitioners points to an application made jointly by the Chairman of the Board of Directors, Progressive Papers Limited, and the Secretary of the Tribune Trust to the Custodian, Punjab, for permission under section 9 of the West Punjab Evacuee Property Protection Act to complete tire sale. The application was sent to the Custodian through the Director of Industries and Rehabilitation Commissioner who made an endorsement on it dated the 22nd June, 1948, that he had no objection to the transfer of the Tribune building and _ the Press with all the machineries, stocks, stores and news-print etc. for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000. The Custodian by his order dated 8th July, 1948 ordered the petition to be registered and issued notice to the Rehabilitation Department. A reference appears to have been made by him to the Ministry of Refugees in reply to which a letter WW. was received from Shawna Shah ab-ud-Din, the then Minister for Refugees. That letter is at page 31 of the file m case No. 30 of 1949. It said that for reasons given by Main Eftekhari- adding, Chairman of the Progressive Papers Limited, he may be permitted to purchase the Tribune Press and this transaction may be treated as a special case. The Custodian recorded the evidence of Mr. Bali, Secretary of the Trust, who stated that the Trust had entered into an agreement for the sale of the Tribune Press, its equipments, fittings, stocks, furniture etc. including a van, for Rs, 1,50,000. The payment was agreed to be made before the Registrar after deducting all payments towards Income-Tax;, electric charges, third party claims, and other charges which had to be paid before the permission could be accorded for completing the sale. The agreement was made in accordance with a resolution passed by the Trustees in their meeting held on the 28th March, 1948, in the interests of the Tribune Trust as it was no longer possible for them to function in Lahore, and they had started bringing out a Tribune Daily newspaper from Ambala Can't. It was considered necessary to sell the property of the Tribune Trust here and purchase property in East Punjab. Mr. Sharma, Manager of the Tribune Trust, deposed that he had been deputed by the Trustees to come to Lahore for the completion of the sale, He had a general power of attorney in his favor for carry mg on the normal business of the Trust but no special power of attorney for executing the sale deed. He said that the Trust was created by the Will of the late Vardar Deal Singh Majestic and there was no specific provision in that Will authorizing the Trustees to sell the property or restrain them from dong so. The Trustees had, however, been disposing of the Trust property in the past without any reference to Court Mr. Amir Hussain Shah, Managing Director of the Progressive Papers Limited, corroborated the statement made by Mr. Bali in his presence. The Custodian then ordered that the requisite clearance certificate and a power of attorney authoring someone to complete the sale should be produced on 2nd July, 1949. The special power of attorney was given by Rai Broader Bari Days to Mr. Sharma and Mr. Bali to execute and register the sale deed. He did so in exercise of the authority conferred upon him by the Trustees and directed the aforesaid attorneys to convey the building, including the open site behind it, and the premises occupied by the Post Office situated on Rattan Hand Road, Lahore, including the Press, office equipment, furniture etc. lying in the aforesaid building for a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 to the Progressive Papers Ltd. The resolutions allowing the sale of the buildings WW. and other moveable property belonging to the Tribune Trust and authorizing Mr. Sharma and Mr. Bali to execute and register the sale deed are on the record. On 2nd July, 1949, Mr. Bali again appeared before the Custodian and said that when the Will was made by Vardar Deal Singh, there was no immovable property attached to the Tribune Trust. The property was acquired later on by the Trustees and that accounted for the omission of any provision in the Will relating to the Trustees’ power to dispose of the property. He produced the special power of attorney and the resolutions above-mentioned. Mr. Amir Hussain Shah produced the clearance certificate from the Income-tax Authority marked Ex. R. A. another from the Property Tax Authority marked Ex. R. B. two from the D. R. C. about the payment of third party clams marked Exes. R. E. 1, and R. E. 2, and the resolution Ex. R. F. signed by the Chairman of the' Progressive Papers Ltd. authorizing him to complete the transaction of sale on their behalf After recording this evidence the Custodian ordered that unless the competency of the Tribune Trust to sell the property was placed beyond doubt by suitable directions from a competent Court further proceedings shall be stayed. On 27th February, 1950, he reviewed his order and said that as the bulk of the consideration for the sale in this case would be absorbed by demands made by the Government and other authorities and as the Tribune Trust was not carrying on any business in Pakistan, their property would have to be sold, sooner or later, to meet the above-mentioned demands and as the purchasers were willing to run the risk BF buying without any specific instructions from a Court there was no necessity to hold up proceedings on the ground that no instructions for sale had been obtained from a Court. In view however, of a Notification by the Pakistan Government dated the 10th January, 1950 he advised the petitioners to approach the Central Government for the removal of the ban on sales contained in the above-mentioned Notification. On 8th April, 1954, the Progressive Papers Limited filed an application under section 15 of Evacuee Property Ordinance and asked for the approval of the Custodian for the completion of the sale in pursuance of the agreement made in 1948. The Habitat'on Authority filed a written statement on 27th May, 1954 opposing the petition but later withdrew the opposition. On 20th May, 1954, letter No. F. (22)/53-R-II, was sent by the Ministry of Refugees and WW. Rehabilitation, Government of Pakistan, to the Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab, referring to the latter’s order dated the 27th February, 1950 and saying that the Chairman, Board of Directors, Progressive Papers Limited had represented to the Ministry that out of the sum of Rs. 1,50,000, the sum of Rs. 56,124-12-0 represented the price of moveable property included in the transaction and the payment made by the Progressive Papers should be considered with reference to the price of the immovable property only, Le. Rs. 1,50,000 minus Rs. 56,124-12-0 Rs. 93,875-4-0. The payments made by the Progressive Papers were shown as under Item Rs. (1) Income-tax 1,04,428-12-0 (2) House-tax 4,049-2-0 (3) Property tax 4,816-7-0 (4) Third party claims 1,669-14-0 (5) Electricity charges 3,323-9-0 (6) Administration charges 7,710-0-0 Total 1,25,997-12-0 The amount paid was stated to be well above the minimum required by the Notification above-mentioned, as amended by Notification No. F. (8)/54-R-II, dated 10th April, 1954, and the Custodian was requested to examine this case IP accordance with the provisions of the last Notification and if the case was considered eligible for completion, it should be ordered to be completed. It may be pointed out here that in clause 20 of the Will of Vardar Deal Singh Militia, it was said that his “property in the stock and good-will of the Tune Press and newspaper in Antral, Lahore” was to vest permanently in a Committee of Trustees consisting of Messes Jitendra Hand Bose, Charles Golan Path, and Harshen All, Barrister-at-Law, and clause 21 provided that it shall be the duty of the said Trustees to maintain the Press and the Newspaper in an efficient condition, keep mg the liberal policy of the said newspaper and devoting the surplus income of the said Press and Newspaper, after defying'all current expenses in improving the said newspaper and placing it on a footing of permanency. In clause 22, which is applicable to all the three Trusts created1 by the donor, it is said that on the death, resignation or disability of any Trustee the remaining Trustees of the Trust concerned shall fill up the vacancy. It appears from clause 20 of the Will that there were no buildings belonging to the Tribune Press or attached to it at the time of the will and all that Vardar Deal Singh owned was the stock and goodwill of the Tribune Press and newspaper in Alkali, Lahore. Counsel for the petitioners states, on instructions received by him, that there was no immovable property attached to the Tribune Press and whatever property now exists was acquired by the Trustees after the Will This statement was made as far back as 2nd July, 1949 before Mr. Justice S. A. Rahman, the then Custodian of WW. Evacuee Property, and the provisions of the Will show that the statement is correct. It has not been controverted by anyone and there is nothing on the record against TT. It is urged by the counsel for the petitioners that the Trustees have always the inherent right to dispose of the Trust property in the interest of the Trust. In this case the Trustees had saved money and built property to Malta the Press and.to put it on a footing of permanency. They had the undoubted right to sell that property if they considered it to be in the interests of the Trust as stated by. Mr. Balt, the Secretary of the Tribune Trust, in his statement dated 31st May, 1949. In Hals bury’s Laws of England, 3rd Edition, Vol. IV, at page 334, it is said that, subject to the restrictions imposed by the Charitable Trusts Act, the Trustees of Charities have power to sell the Charity estates upon their own initiative, whether expressly authorized by the instrument of Trust or not, provided that the sale is in the interests of this charity. In Law Report 1911-Chancery Division, page 442, it is said that ordinarily a direction to Trustees to invest in particular investments implies a power to vary the investments and that implied power gives the Trustees the power to sell real estate. In the Commentaries under section 22 of the Trust Act by Aggarwal, IST Edition, page 261, it is stated that where there are no special directions to sell in the Instrument creating the Trust, the Trustees may sell under circumstances which render a sale necessary. In Onward Doorganath Roy v. Ram Chunder Sen (1) it was held by the Privy Council that the Manager of an estate had the power to raise money by alienating a part of that estate if the purposes of the endowment required it. A Division Bench of the Madras High Court held in Kuttayakath Via Karma v. Brinjal Karaganda Flappy (2) that though, ordinarily, a Trustee of a temple should not alienate the crops of the Trust by way of mortgage or sale and'” should try to raise the sum required for necessary purposes of the temple, such as repairs etc. by public subscriptions or by curtailment of other expenses, yet an alienation made by the Trustee for such a purpose is perfectly valid. Instances can be multiplied whereby it can be shown that a Trustee, for the proper discharge of his duties, must have the meant power of disposal over the Trust property. For example, suppose a Trust property is burnt to ashes. It was insured, according to the price of the building at the time of the construction, for only Rs. 25,0OD. The cost of building having gone up in recent y ears, the reconstruction of the property would cost Rs. 50,000. Will not the Trustees have the right to borrow Rs. 25,000 oh the security of that property in order to rebuild it and repay the amount borrowed from the future rent of the property. This would be an act of good WW. management, and it would be a failure of duty on the part of the Trustees to let the site lie waste and the Trust to die. The R. O. (Legal) has not been able to show that the Trustees cannot dispose of the Trust property if it is in the merest, of the Trust. I am of the opinion that the Trustees had the right to enter into an agreement for the sale of this property. The only question is whether it was in the interest of the Trust. And I should give my approval or not. As stated above, the Central Government and the Rehabilitation are in favor of the approval being granted and the sale being sanctioned. There is nothing to show that the agreement to sell was not in the interest of the Trust as it was stated to be by the Secretary of the Trust. No Law nor any other cause has been shown against the approval being given, and I give the approval asked for under section 15 of the Evacuee Property Ordinance for the execution and registration of the. sale deed in question. A. H., Transfer approved. w.

According to section 6, para. 2, of the Evacuee Property Ordinance any evacuee property which is held in Trust for religious or charitable purposes shall remain vested in the Custodian only till such time as fresh trustees are apported in the manner provided by Law and pending the appointment of fresh trustees the Trust property and the income thereof shall be applied by the Custodian for fulfilling as far as possible, the purposes of the Trust. The question arises whether the Custodian can, during the time when he is in charge of the property, sell the property or he can merely use it for the -purposes of the Trust. Counsel for the petitioners says that in this case the property is already under an agreement of sale made by the Trustees and the Custodian is asked merely to give his approval to that contract. This gives rise to the next question whether, the Trustees had, after they had become evacuees, any power to make a contract in respect of this property. The answer to this question is that there was nothing to prevent them from making a contract, but the contract cannot be enforced without the permission of the Custodian. Section 15 of the Evacuee Property Ordinance prohibits the transfer of property, in areas relating to which a Notification has been issued, except with the previous approval in writing of the Custodian. If the Custodian gives his approval to the completion of this contract, the Trustees have the power to complete the sale ; otherwise not. Section 16 says that no creation or transfer of any right or merest in or encumbrance upon any property made in any manner whatsoever, on or after the first day of March, 1947, by or on behalf of any evacuee or by or on behalf of a person \Who has or may hereafter become an evacuee after the date of such creation or transfer shall be effective so as to confer any right or remedy on any party thereto or on any

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 1955 PLD 5.
Answer: A. M. Jan (Custodian).-This is a petition under section 13-A of the Rehabilitation Ordinance (XIX of 1948) against an order allotting shop No. 72 situated on The Mall Lahore in favor of Messes Nazi Baths Sons of 26 Mc Load Road Lahore. The facts of the case are that on 30th December 1947, this shop was allotted to one Aftab Lodi. He later on took a partner named Mamdani, but it appears that their business did not prosper and on 12th September 1953 they made an application to the D. R. C. Lahore that they were willing to surrender the allotment of this shop in favor of Amir Ahmad Khan, one of the partners of Syed Thais Ltd. who was stated in the petition to be a refugee from Meerut. On the same day ZAM Ahmad Khan made an application to the D. R. C. Lahore on behalf of his firm, Syed Thais Ltd. showing that they were very well off in Meerut put had fallen on evil days owing to Partition. They added that Mr. Aftab Lodi and Mr. Mamdani, Proprietors of the International Trading Corporation, were willing to surrender possession of the shop to the petitioners and prayed that the shop may be allotted to them. The D. R. C. asked for a report from the R. O. Civil Lines who reported that Mr. Aftab Lodi and his partner Mr. Mamdani said that hey had lost about thirty thousand rupees in their business and were unable to carry on anymore. They were, therefore, prepared to surrender possession of the shop in favor of Syed Thais Ltd. who were financially sound and recommended for the allotment of the shop. The D. R. C. Lahore, vide his order dated 21st September 1953, accepted the recommendation and allotted the shop to Syed Thais Ltd. On the next day Syed Thais Ltd. bought over the furniture, fittings and stock belonging to the International Trading Corporation, entered in the list marked A, for Rs. 7,500 as shown in receipt marked B. After about a month the petitioners received a letter from the Rehabilitation Officer, Civil Lines, directing them to appear before the Rehabilitation Commissioner (General) on 26th October 1953 in connection with this shop. Mr. Amir Ahmad Khan appeared on behalf of Syed Thais in the Court of the Rehabilitation Commissioner on 26th October 1953, but the case was adjourned to 5th November 1953 When the Rehabilitation Commissioner cancelled the allotment in favor of the petitioners of the ground that it had been alleged that Mr. Amir. Ahmad Khan had got this shop by paying part, Mr. ZAM Ahmad Khan’s contention that he had paid Rs. 7,500 for the goods purchased by him as shown MN the list and the receipt above-mentioned was not taken any notice of: No one who may have made the allegation that this money was paid as part was named or examined by the R. C. (G) but he held the allotment in favor of the petitioners to be suspicious and directed the premises to be sealed within three days during which the petitioners were required to remove their property and the shop was ordered to be advertised for allotment. The petitioner too were allowed to apply and they did so. Mr. Amir Ahmad Khan however, made a representation to the Central Government against the order of the R. C. (G) and the Central Government wrote to the R, C. (G) that the petitioners had complained that the charges on account of which their allotment was cancelled had not been properly considered or proved. It was added in the letter mentioned above, No. Dy. -MRI dated IST April 1954, that the petitioner was a bona fide refugee who had suffered considerable loss in India for which he had not been compensated, that he had invested a substantial amount of money in the business he was carrying on in No. 72, The Mall Lahore, that his case should be reconsidered, and it should be made sure that a settled refugee is not unsettled on mere suspicion. In another letter dated 12th April 1954, the Central Government asked the Rehabilitation Commissioner to submit a full report relating to the facts of this case. On 2nd June 1954 the R. C. (G) wrote to the Central Government and undertook to submit the report called for but somehow forgot to do so and oh 13th July 1954 allotted the shop in question to the respondents Messes. Nazi Baths Sons, without any reference to the Central Government, and ordered that the petitioners should be ejected and all applicants for allotment should be informed that the shop had been allotted to the, respondents. On 17th July 1954 the Central Government sent a reminder to the R. C. (G) asking for the report promised in his letter dated 2nd June 1954. On the same day, 1e. 17th July 1954, the petitioners filed a petition for revision against the order of the R. C. (G) in my Court and prayed for postponement of ejectment proceedings. This prayer was granted, and the case was fixed for hearing on 29th July 1954. On 27th July 1954 the Central Government sent an express telegram asking me to postpone the hearing of the case because Mr. Amir Ahmad Khan had asked for time to collect evidence which he wished to produce before me. A copy of the representation made by him was sent to me with the telegram and postponed the case to enable the petitioners to produce the evidence. They have produced copies of the above-mentioned letters from the Central Government. They were sent to me by the Musty of Refugees and Rehabilitation at the request of the petitioner because the file of the case in the R. C. (G.s) Office was either destroyed or stolen. Messes. Nazi Baths Sons, the new allottees, made an application that they should be made a party to this case and I allowed that by order dated 20th October 1954. The case for the petitioners was argued by Mr. Aqua Ali Khan who emphasized that there was no evidence whatsoever that the petitioners had paid any part or bribe to the previous allottees, that the sum of Rs. 7,500 paid by them was the price of the goods purchased as shown in the list and the receipt marked A and B, that the order for the petitioner’s ejectment from shop No. 72 was wholly unwarranted and based upon no evidence, that it was highly undesirable to unsettle a settled refugee on mere suspicion as posted out by the Central Government, that the petitioners had applied for allotment as directed by the R. C. (G)and R. C. (G’s) Order, dated 13th July 1954, allotting the shop to Messes Nazi Baths Sons was unjust and showed no reason why preference was given to Nazi Baths Sons over the petitioners who were in lawful possession of the shop by order of the D. R. C. dated 21st September 1953. It was further urged that the petitioners had spent about Rs. 10,000 on repairing the shop and had invested a large sum of money in buying the'stock, furniture and fittings of the old allottees and a great deal of new stock. They were already ruined by the losses suffered in India and if the business now built up by them is allowed to be ruled by the Rehabilitation Department, which was set up to help the refugees, there would be no hope of the petitioners’ survival. The points urged by the counsel for the respondents are (1) that the partnership between Aftab Lodi and Mamdani was never recognized by the Rehabilitation Authority, (2) that the petitioners did not say in their application for allotment dated 12th September 1953 that they had agreed to buy the stock of the previous allottees, though several days before this application the Rehabilitation Authority had been informed by the respondents that Hamadan was asking for a part. Neither post has any force or relevancy. Whether the partnership between Aftab Lodi and Mamdani was recognized by the Rehabilitation Authority or not has any bearing on the allotment in favor of the petitioners made by the Rehabilitation Authority on 21st September 1953 and the fact that the Rehabilitation Authority had been informed that Mamdani was asking for a part merely shows that they had been warned before the allotment in favor of the petitioners. It is interesting to note that the letter dated 25th August 1953, marked C, in which the information about the part was given by the respondents to the Rehabilitation Commissioner (General) does not say that the. petitioners had offered any part to Aftab Lodi or Hamadan. On the contrary, it is said that the respondents had offered Mamdani Rs. 9,000 as part, but he was not prepared to take anything less than Rs. 15,000. Their offer of Rs. 9,000 as part to the previous allottees was relied upon by the respondents to show the extent of their need for this shop, and it was prayed that the shop should be immediately allotted to them. This letter does not show any malpractice on the part of the petitioners though it does on the part of the respondents. It was not necessary for the petitioners to state in their application for allotment that they had agreed to buy the stock MN trade of the previous allottees. This was a matter between them and the previous allottees and depended upon the shop being allotted to the petitioners. When it was allotted to them, they purchased the goods belonging to the previous allottees. This was a perfectly legal contract and there was nothing improper about it. There had been a good deal of confused thinking regarding what is popularly called part. It can be described as a consideration paid by a person to an allottee for giving the allotted property, wholly or partially, to the person making the payment. The payment of such consideration is not recognized as AF ground for allotment by the Rehabilitation Authority and claim to! possession based on such payment is not accepted. The allottees of evacuee property do not acquire any right to allot that property to others and as soon as the allotment relating to a property comes to an end, either by the efflux of time or abandonment, the property becomes subject to a fresh allotment by the Rehabilitation Authority. In this case the petitioners do not claim possession of the shop because they have paid any part to the previous allottees ; nor because they have purchased the stock-in-trade of the previous allottees. There is no evidence whatsoever that the petitioners had paid any part to the! previous allottees, and the purchase of stock and goods was a perfectly legal transaction. Even if the petitioners had paid part it would have; made no difference because their claim to possession is not based on the willingness of the previous allottees to surrender possession in the! Favor but upon a valid order of allotment passed on 21st September! 1953, by the Rehabilitation Authority. There is no allegation nor proof that the Rehabilitation Authority had received any part for making the allotment. The Rehabilitation Commissioner (General) has stated in his order dated Sth November 1953 that there were instructions that shops on The Mall should not be allotted without the previous approval of the Rehabilitation Commissioner. He, therefore, cancelled the allotment and ordered fresh applications to be invited. The petitioners applied again in obedience to this order and so did some others but without showing any reason why preference was given to the respondents, over the other applicants the shop was allotted to the respondents. Only the petitioners have come up in revision which shows that the other applicants are not interested in the shop and, in any case, the time within which they could have applied for revision has expired and the order of the Rehabilitation Commissioner (General) has become final against them. I he choose, therefore, lies between the petitioners and the respondents. Under section 13-A subsection Rehabilitation Ordinance, a revision petition against the order of a Rehabilitation Commissioner can be disposed of by the Central Government or by such officer as it may apport from time to time in this behalf: The Central Government has appointed the Custodian of Evacuee Property to dispose of such petitions. The power to dispose of implies the power to make allotment MN favor of any of the parties to the petition. It is well established law that when once the jurisdiction to revise is established there is no imitation imposed on the power of the revising! Court regarding the mode of disposal. The revising Court may finally dispose of the case itself or pass any other order which may satisfy the! ends of justice. Several authorities on this post are given in Note 16 of Chita ley’s. Commentaries on the Civil Procedure Code under section 115 which relates to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court. In Lab Singh v. Aim Din (Civil Revision No. 792 of 1930), published in the appellate Court had acted without jurisdiction and Ten Hand, J. held that in revision there were three courses open to him: (1) to refuse to interfere info injustice had been done, (2) to set aside the judgment and return the appeal for presentation to the proper Court, and (3) to go through the record and decide the case himself. He found they,t Justice had been done in that case and did not consider (1) AI R 1931 LAH. P. 748. it proper to remand the case as it meant subjecting the parties to further expenses of litigation the lower courts and possibly again in the High Court. He, therefore, went through the case and decided it himself: I too, after gong through the record and hearing the counsel for both sides, find that injustice has been done to the petitioners in this case, and it will not be fair to send the case back to the Rehabilitation Commissioner for advertising the shop once again and inviting fresh applications for allotment. The petitioners are refugees and entitled to the allotment of this shop. They have invested a large sum of money in the business that they are carrying on here and there is no reason for ejecting them. I, therefore, cancel the allotment in favor of the respondents and order that the petitioners shall remain in peaceful possession of this shop so long as they abide by the terms of allotment in their favor. If the respondents are also refugees and in need of shop they should apply to the Rehabilitation Authority whose duty it is to bring about the orderly settlement of refugees. The petition for revision is accepted. A. H Petition acc épée d WWW.

The same will be examined for initiating suitable action in accordance with law, if so watranted." 2. Pursuant to the above short order, we tend to record the supporting reasons. The brief facts are that on 11-5-1998 India exploded three nuclear devices. Then on 13-5-1998, it farther exploded two more nuclear devices. The ; above explosions of nuclear devices generated in Pakistan a lot of anxiety, particularly on account of hostile and aggressive postures of the Indian political leaders which they adopted after the above explosions. There was much debate orally as well as in writing through press articles on the question, whether Pakistan should also give a befitting reply to India by carrying out its own nuclear device tests. The international leaders including Bill Clinton, President of U.S.A. Tony Beam, Prime Minister of U.K. and Jacques Chirac, President of France, impressed upon the Prime Munster of Pakistan not to retaliate India's above’ unwarranted and uncalled-for action of exploding above nuclear devices. However, eventually keeping in -view the interest of the country and the demand of the people of Pakistan, the Government of Pakistan conducted five nuclear device tests on 28- 5-1998. On the evening of the same day, the Proclamation of Emergency under Article 233 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as the Constitution) was issued. On the same day the President of Pakistan also issued an Order under clause (2) of Article 233 of the Constitution suspending all the Fundamental Rights. The above Proclamation of Emergency and the Order of suspension of Fundamental Rights were assailed before this Court through direct Constitution Petitions under Article 184(3) of the Constitution, which culminated in the judgment rendered on 13-10-1998 inter alia in the case of Vardar Farooq Ahmad Khan [ Safari and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others PLD 1999 SC 57, whereby it was held that the issuance of Proclamation under clause (1) of Article 232 of the Constitution was valid, but the order of suspending the Fundamental Rights under clause of Article 233 was not valid and warranted under the Constitution/law. WW. It may be observed that on the above same day (i.e. 28-5- 1998) the Foreign Exchange (Temporary Restrictions),Ordinance, 1998 was promulgated.
