Question: Provide the full judgment for case 2016 PLD 46.
Answer: SARDAR ABDUL HAMMED KHAN, J.- Through the above captioned petitions filed under Section 44 of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act, 1974, the petitioners seek abrogation of clause of rules 3 and 14 of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Sale and Development of Private Forest Rules, 2001, issued vide notification bearing No.F/S/6296- dated 16.10.2001 being against the constitutional provisions and their vested legal rights. 2. Brief and common facts resulting into the filing of the above titled petitions, as per claim of the petitioners are that they are First Class subjects of the State of Azad Jammu and Kashmir and are also owners of the private forests in their native villages. It has been stated that the Government of Azad Jammu and Kashmir vide notification bearing No.1051-75 dated 13.03.1984, framed rules for regulating the private forests. These rules were challenged before this Court by filing writ petition. This Court vide judgment dated 20.10.2000 in the case titled Vardar Inapt Khan v. Azad Govt, and others, accepted the petition, nullified the impugned rules and directed the concerned authorities, with certain guidelines to frame new rules. The Azad Government, in compliance of the judgment of this Court, promulgated new rules vide notification dated 16.10.2001. According to the new rules, number of trees was reduced from 25 to 18 for the trees having above 22 inches diameter and 200 to 100 for the thinning trees. A limit of the timber to be sold by the owners of a private forest was also fixed in the above rules. The petitioners have assailed the said rules on the ground that the number of trees 1e 18 or more of 22 or more diameter and 100 thinning trees is against the fundamental rights of the forests owners, enshrined under the Interim Constitution. Condition of sale of the timber has also been challenged on the same ground. 3. The respondents were summoned for filing comments and later on written statement and the needful has been done, accordingly. In the within statement, the claim of the petitioners has been refuted, totally, and it has been stated that the number of trees has been reduced on the direction of the High Court and maximum number has been fixed, in order to declare, a forest as private forest. It is further stated that the forests having lesser number of the trees do not fall m the definition of the private forests and usage of such forests on commercial basis will be harmful not only for the State but also to the forest owners. It has been claimed that if the owners of the forests are allowed to sale out their forests in any way and manner, the same will deteriorate the environment of the area as well as the life of the dams will be reduced due to dumping of soil. The respondents have stated that if the forest owners are allowed to sell their forests without any limit, it will destroy the forests of the State in a merciless manner. It is also stated that the rules under challenge have been framed in light of the guidelines laid down by this Court m Vardar Inapt's case decided on 20.10.2000. 4. Syed Nazi Hussain Shah Nazi Advocate, the learned counsel for the petitioners, in his written arguments has contended that the petitioners are lawful owners of the land under the private forest and the revenue department has issued N.O. Cs in their favor. It has been contended that Azad Jammu and Kashmir Government, initially framed rules for regularization of the private forests known as AJ&K Sales and Development of Private Forests Rules, 1984, which were challenged before this court through Constitutional writ petition and the court has directed the government to frame new rules keeping in view the fundamental rights of the subjects of the State enshrined in the Interim Constitution Act, 1974. The learned counsel has contended that Azad Jammu and Kashmir Government framed rules by avoiding the guidelines laid down by this court and enforced the same on 16.10.2001. The learned counsel stated that existing rules have been framed in derogation with the Interim Constitution Act, 1974 and rules 3 and 14 of the said rules are liable to be struck down. It has been stated that under rule 3(1) of the said rules minimum number of the trees above 22" diameter is 18 and the number of thinning trees is 100. Hence, rule 3 of the earlier rules and that of the prevailing rules are same. Similarly, under rule 14 of the existing rules only 2 lac cubic feet timber from conifer trees and 20000 efts from broad leaves trees can be marked, and this restriction is against the fundamental rights of the private forest owners. The learned counsel has ma'am;gained that the owners of the private forests have not been heard before promulgation of the new rules hence the same are liable to be set at naught. Finally the learned counsel has craved for acceptance of the writ petitions, reversal of the impugned rules and a direction to the respondents for framing new rules in consultation, with the private forests owners and referred the following case law: 1. 2005 SCR 236. 2. 1993 PLC (C.S.) 1201. 3. PLD 1998 SC(AJ&K) 17. 4.2003 PLC (C:S.) 1 5. Raja Ahead Ali Khan Advocate, the learned legal Advisor for the forest department has filed written arguments stating therein that the petitioners do not fall within the definition of aggrieved persons, and they have no locus standi to file the above writ petitions. It has been argued that the petitions are hit by latches as the rules under challenge have been enforced in 2001 whereas, the petitions have been filed in 2004. The learned counsel has argued that no constitutional or legal right of the petitioners has been infringed and the rules under challenge have been framed in compliance of the court order as well as keeping in view the guidelines laid down by this court in Vardar Inapt Khan's case. The learned counsel has contended that the number of trees to be marked; either 22" or above diameter or the thinning trees has been reduced from 25 to 18 and 200 to 100 respectively. Referring to rule 14 of the impugned rules the learned counsel has contended that the restriction on sale of the prescribed quantity of the timber has been fixed keeping in view the consequences of the cutting of the trees at a large scale which may cause destruction of the environment as well as the dams. It has been maintained by the learned ‘counsel that the Inter Constitution Act does not contain any restriction regarding promulgation of rules and regulations for regularizing the private businesses hence, the impugned rules are not derogatory to the said Act. Finally, the learned counsel has craved for dismissal of the writ petitions with costs, 6. We have examine4 the written arguments filed by the learned counsel for the parties, perused the record made available with the file and considered the controversy with due care. 7. It may be stated that the rules under challenge have been framed in compliance of the judgment passed by this Court in case titled Vardar Inapt Khan v. Azad Jammu and Kashmir Government and others' Writ Petition No. decided on 20.10.2000. In the earlier rules, the number of trees having 22 inches or more diameter was fixed as 25 and the number of thinning trees, poles was 200. The rules were challenged, and the learned bench seized with the matter, while accepting the petition, directed the respondents, therein, to frame new rules keeping in view the guidelines, laid down therein. 8. Before adverting to the merits of the case we would like to reproduce the relevant excerpts from the repealed rules 1984, rules under challenge, 2001, guidelines and findings returned by this court in the above referred case. "Rules 1984, Rule 3. The sale of the private forest shall be sanctioned by the Government: Provided that 25 trees or more of over 22" diameter at breast height are available under the selection-cum improvement system or 200 poles or more available underthinning, and AKS-LATHA" of the area is available with the Revenue Department. Rule 14. Sale DF wood from private forest Ina year shall not exceed two lac efts. Of conifers and twenty thousand efts; of broad leaved trees in standing volume, through-out Azad Jammu and Kashmir territory. No suit shall he against any Government servant for any loss or any act done by him m good faith; provided it is not done willfully, maliciously, negligently or intentionally to harm the owner or exploitation agency." Rules, 2001 Rule 3. The sale of private forests shall be sanctioned by the Chief Conservator of Forests subject to fulfilling the following conditions but total period consuming and Lodging a request by the applicant till the grant of final sanction to start with marketing the timber shall not exceed one-year period: (i) Eighteen trees or more. Of 22 inches and above diameter at the breast height are available under the selection cum-improvement system or 100 poles (above 8 inches DBH) or more available under thinning, and AKS-LATHA (Field map) of the area is available with the revenue Department. (i) The forest will be worked under selection-cum improvement system with a felling cycle of at least ten years. (i!) For broad leaved trees the concerned DFO will decide its exploitation under silvicultural. (iv) Private Forest trees affected by natural calamities and public projects shall be excluded from the operation of section 3(1) due to unavoidable circumstances. Rule (14). Throughout the territory of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, sale of wood from private forests in a year shall not exceed two lac eft on conifers and twenty thousand efts of broad leaved trees in standing volume. 9. A careful perusal of the files reveals that the rules enforced by the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Government have been challenged by the petitioners on the ground that the same have not been framed in light of the guidelines laid down by this Court in Vardar Inapt Khan's case. For convenience, the guidelines, laid down in the above referred case are reproduced, which are as follows:- a) Application may be made to the Chief Conservator Forests; b) The Deputy Commissioner after due inquiry should issue the certificate of undisputed ownership and possession within 3 months; c) The approval by the competent authority may be issued within further 3 months; d) The marking on spot of the trees should not take more than two months. This period may however, extended in the snow fall areas or where there is a war like condition; e) The option should lie with the owner to undertaking the job himself under the supervision of Forests Department; f) Provision should be made for reasonable expenses of the department at the costs of the owner for services of the staff g) Reasonable amount of the royalty should also be paid to the Government; h) Thus, in all cases the total period in starting the marketing of the timber should not extend one year." 10. A perusal of the files also reveals that the moot ports in the controversy are; whether, the rules. Under challenge have been framed according to the guidelines laid down by this Court and whether, the fundamental rights of the petitioners, granted in the Interim Constitution Act, 1974 have been infringed or not? In this regard, we would like to reproduce, the relevant provisions of the Act, which are as follows: Selection Fundamental Rights 8. Freedom of trade, business or profession:- Every State subject possessing such qualifications, if any, as may be prescribed by law in relation to his profession or occupation shall have the right to enter upon any lawful profession or occupation, and to conduct any lawful trade or business. Provided that nothing in this paragraph shall prevent- a) The regulation of any trade or profession by a licensing system; or b) The regulation of trade, commerce or industry in the interest of free competition therein; or (c) The carrying on, by Government or council, or by a corporation controlled by Government or the council, of any trade, business, industry or service, to the exclusion, complete or partial, or other persons. 13. Provision as to property:- Subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the public interest, every State Subject shall have the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property. 14. Protection of Property:- (1) No person shall be deprived of his property save in accordance with law. Explanation: In sub-paragraphs (2) and 'property' shall mean immovable property, or any commercial or industrial undertaking or any interest in any undertaking. 11. This Court is in agreement with the claim of the petitioners that each and every State Subject has an equal right hold, acquire and utilize the property owned by him, but the same is subject to some restrictions, like safeguard of the rights of the other subjects, public interest etc. and nobody can be allowed to carry on his business or utilize his property, according to his wishes Ina free laces manner. An owner of some property or business may run his business or utilize his property keeping in view the rights of the other subjects as well as the public interest; moreover all these rights are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law as postulated in supra quoted constitutional provisions. For judging the reasonability of the impugned rules we have scanned the impugned rules as well the pleadings and other record of both the writ petitions. 12. The respondents in their written statement, while referring Rule 14 of the impugned rules, have stated as under:- 13. The controversy relating to violation of fundamental right was resolved by the apex Court of AJ&K in case titled AKLASC and 6 others v. AJ&K Govt, and 8 others [2000 YLR 2911], Relevant observation which reads as under:- "A Notification was issued on 16th May 1997 that the President of Azad Jammu and Kashmir had accorded approval to a decision taken by the Cabinet to impose complete ban on cutting, of trees on commercial basis for a period of three years. It was also notified that no tender will be cited for cutting of trees nor would any contract be awarded. All contracts relating to Forest Department and Azad Jammu Kashmir Logging and Saw Mills Corporation in which work orders had been issued, but actual work had not commenced were cancelled. Seven persons, Gular Ahmed Abbas and others filed a writ petition on 19th June 1997 seeking a declaration that the Notification mentioned above had been issued without lawful authority. Some notices issued to the writ petitioners to stop their respective works were also challenged. They also prayed for a writ of prohibition restraining the respondents, Azad Government of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, Forest Department and AKLAS Corporation from interfering in the execution of their works. The writ petition was accepted on 3rd April 1998 but with certain conditionalities which are unacceptable to the contractors. Two main grounds were urged in the writ petition. The first ground was the impugned Notification was inconsistent with Fundamental Rights No. (FREEDOM OF TRADE, BUSINESS OR PROFESSION}, No. 13 PROVISION AS TO PROPERTY and PROTCTION OF PROPERTY No. 14 The second post was that the Executive did not enjoy the power to issue the Notification because it is only the Legislature which can deprive a person of his property which can be done in accordance with law. The main plank of the arguments was that the impugned Notification had deprived the writ petitioners of the "property" within the meaning of Fundamental Right, No. 14 and was therefore void. "This definition does not say what property is but only lays down that the term property includes, inter alia right or interest in moveable or immovable property and means of production. It is an accepted fact that meaning of property is very wide. It is provided in sub-paragraph (1) of Fundamental Right No. 14 that no person shall be deprived of his property save in accordance with law. The definition of property given at the end of the Fundamental Right is not applicable to sub-paragraph Therefore the extended definition, reproduced above, in section 2 1s applicable. As concluded above, the interests of the contractors were covered by this definition and, therefore, they could not be deprived of it save in accordance with law as authoritatively laid in Kashmir Timber Corporation case." 13(sic). It may be proper to mention that the impugned rules have been framed in the light of earlier judgment of this court recorded in Analyst Khan’s case. It is admitted fact that “the Rules are part of the law as these carry out the purpose of law and regulate the business to be conducted under the law. These have the same force as the law has. The law is not one man business nor is to be made to benefit anyone. The framing and promulgation of the law or rules is a institutional function of a state or Government as the case may be. All the departments which are concerned with the framing of law or rules have to go through the process provided for framing or amending the law and rules as the case may be. While keeping in mind the above principle of law framing process, we have analyzed the impugned provision of rules along with the explanation /reasons furnished by the respondents in their pleadings but have no reason to differ with the view post of respondents, because we are fully cognizant of the environmental requirements of the state in the context of Global Environmental crises which is the most burning issue of whole the world. It may be added that this is the era of environmental protection efforts and law relating thereto. 14. It may further be observed that while examine the reasonability of rules in view of provisions of fundamental right No. 13 of Interim Constitution Act 1974, regarding imposition of "reasonable restrictions" pertaining to right, to acquire hold and dispose of property. We have given our earnest thought to the controversy, and we are of the firmed view that "right to acquire, hold and dispose of property’, can be regulated only through reasonable restrictions imposed by law in public interest. Both validity of law and action taken become justiciable from standpoint of the reasonableness as well as public interest. If restriction to hold properly imposed by law is found reasonable, court would uphold the same. We felt satisfied, that the restrictions imposed are reasonable and not warrant any interference. This view of the Court is also fortified by 2003 CLD 1797, 15. In continuation of the above we have categorically noted that vide clause (1) of the rule 3, the quantity of trees of 22"(twenty-two inches) diameter has been reduced from 25 to 18 as well as the quantity of 200 poles has been reduced to 100 poles. Moreover, omission of clause regarding non-institution of the suit against the Government Servant in Rule 14 are the major changes which is seen collectively, are almost in line with guidelines given in the ibid judgment of this Court. Hence, it may safely be concluded that the restrictions imposed in the impugned’ rules are fully covered under the definition of "reasonable restrictions" which have been imposed in "the public interest" it is further observed that the public interact is the supreme merest. Thus it is concluded that neither violation of any law nor contravention of any constitutional provision or infringement of any fundamental right has been found in the cases in hand. 16. The nub of the above discussion is that both the above captioned writ petitions, having no merits are hereby dismissed, with no order as to costs. Petitions dismissed. WWW

Moreover, omission of clause regarding non-institution of the suit against the Government Servant in Rule 14 are the major changes which is seen collectively, are almost in line with guidelines given in the ibid

Question: Provide the full judgment for case .
Answer: MIAN SAQIB NISAR, J. - The suit for declaration etc. filed by the respondent-plaintiff against the appellant-defendant, after the contest and trial, was decreed by the learned Civil Judge, Swabia vide judgment and decree dated 3.7.2002 holding that the house in dispute has been validly transferred to the respondent by'the Evacuee Department, and it has not been established by the appellant to be attached to any charitable/religious trust etc. to form part of an evacuee trust property. However, on the crucial objection, raised ‘appellant WIFI had culminated into issue No. it was ostensibly found by the Trial Court having no " jurisdiction in the matter, yet strangely the suit as mentioned earlier was decreed. The appeal of the appellant, which was filed through Assistant Administrator, Evacuee Trust Property, Peshawar, was dismissed by the Additional District Judge on 5.3.2003 while upholding the decision of the Trial Court as a whole, and for an additional reason that the appeal was instituted by an officer, who was not competent to do so: these judgments and decrees have been sustained by the Peshawar High Court through its judgment dated 19.12.2003. Leave to appeal was granted in this case on 26.1.2006 in the following terms:- "Contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner is that the suit filed by the respondent/plaintiff was barred by law as such Civil Court has no jurisdiction to grant the declaration prayed for n view of the bar contained in Section 14 of the Evacuee Trust Properties (Management and Disposal) Act XIII of 1975 and such plea was raised before the Trial Court and as such issue was also framed and finding of the suit on Issue No. was to the effect that the Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, yet the suit was decreed and declaration was granted declaring the suit property to be non-evacuee". 2. The brief facts germane for the disposal of the present appeal, are: the house in question measuring about four Marley, situated m village Aida (Swabia) was transferred to the respondent by the Assistant Settlement Commissioner (Lands), Marian through PTO dated 6.10.1967 on the payment of Rs. 1010/-. On the strength of the above, the respondent on 13.6.1996 brought the suit seeking declaration about his exclusive ownership of the house and asserting that the appellant has no right or concern thereto with an additional claim of permanent injunctive relief that the appellant should not meddle, with his ownership and possessory rights qua the suit property. The appellant in its written statement took up the specific objection regarding the jurisdiction of the Civil Court to entertain and try the suit which objection obviously was in terms of Section 14 read with other enabling provisions of Evacuee Trust Properties (Management and Disposal) Act (XIII), 1975 (hereafter referred to as the Act). It may be pertinent to mention here that in the first instance the learned Civil Judge seized of the case vide order dated 3.4.2000, rejected the plaint of the respondent under Order 7, Rule 11, CPC holding that it has no jurisdiction to hear the matter, which (jurisdiction) 1s barred by law. The respondent preferred an appeal which was allowed and by setting aside the order impugned therein, the case was remanded with the direction that such objection should form into an issue and should be decided along with other issues evolved in the matter. Upon trial, the learned Civil Judge on the issue of jurisdiction has come to the conclusion "in the light of above discussion, it is held that this Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the mutant suit. [his issue is therefore decided in positive" (emphasis supplied). It may be relevant to mention here that from the reproduced part of the findings of the Trial Court and of the leave granting order, an impression can be gathered that the Civil Judge seized of the matter decided the issue of jurisdiction against the respondent and yet decreed the suit. But upon reading of the specific wordings of issue No. 1e. "whether this Court has no jurisdiction to restrain (sic) the present suit Our view is otherwise, because the discussion on this issue by the Trial Court especially the portion "the objection with respect to bar of jurisdiction under Section 14 TTB, B (sic) Act, 1975 appears to have no force" leads us to form an opinion that the finding is, that the Court has the jurisdiction. Be that as it may, the revisional Court (the High Court) having final say in the matter by relying upon the judgment of this Court reported as Evacuee Trust Property Board through Assistant Administrator, Evacuee Trust Property Board at Mirpur Khas v. Abdul Aziz Khan and 6 others (2000 SCMR 1371) particularly by quoting a portion therefrom Le. Since in Jaw the disputed property had not been treated as evacuee trust property, therefore, the bar of jurisdiction cannot be pressed into service. For the ouster of jurisdiction, the petitioner ought to have proved through cogent evidence that the disputed property was attached to a charitable trust and as such no suit was maintainable in respect thereof” Therefore, on the touchstone of the above and while examining the documentary evidence, produced by the appellant9 the revisional Court came to the conclusion that from none of such documents it is established if either the suit property was declared to be an evacuee trust property by the Chairman or was ever so treated; and/or even e said documents do not relate to the suit property It is therefore, on account of this that the decisions of the two Courts were upheld by dismissing the revision petition of the appellant. Learned counsel for the appellant states that in terms of Section 8 of the Act that it is the exclusive jurisdiction of the Chairman, Evacuee Trust Property Board to adjudge, decide and declare whether any property is an evacuee trust property or not; besides the validation of certain transfers of the properties which are considered to be evacuee trust properties shall also be within the sole and exclusive empowerment of the Chairman and the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts in relation to these powers/questions is expressed barred by the two noted provisions of law. Further by making Reference to Section 14 of the Act, it is submitted that there is an express bar for the exercise of the jurisdiction by the Civil Court in respect of any action which an officer appointed under the Act is empowered determine or to take or to be taken in exercise of any power conferred upon him by or under the Act. In support of submissions, he has also relied upon the cases reported! as Evacuee Trust Property Board and others v. Ahmed and others (2004 SCMR 440), Evacuee Trust Property Board and others v. MST. Sabina Bibi and others (2007 SCMR 262) Sugar Department through Chief Administrator, USAF Punjab, Lahore v. Secretary, Ministry of Religious Zakat, User and Minorities Affairs, Government of Pakistan, Islamabad and 3 others (2009 SCMR 210) and Evacuee Trust Property Board v. Sheikh Abdul Attar and another (2009 SCMR 1.223). Whereas, contrary to the above-learned counsel for the respondent, has relied upon 2000 SCMR 1371 (supra) the judgment on which reliance has been placed by the High Court. 4. Heard. From the above-mentioned provisions of the Act and the case-law cited, it is clear that for the actions/orders etc. mentioned in the Section, an express bar has been placed upon the exercise of jurisdiction by the Civil Courts. However, when the facts of the present case are exam med in the light of the evidence brought on the record by the parties particularly the appellant, it has conspicuously emerged that no declaration under Section 8 of the Act assigning the suit property a status of evacuee trust property has been made by the Chairman, Evacuee Trust Property Board. Likewise, the validity of the transfer made in favor of the respondent by the evacuee department through the PTO referred to above has not been determined and adjudicated by the Chairman as required under Section 10 of the Act. Obviously, in such a situation the specific bar contemplated by the noted two Sections shall not be attracted. As regards, the general bar of Section 14 is concerned, on the basis of which leave was granted by this Court, it (the Section) reads as under:- Bar of jurisdiction. Save as otherwise provided in this Act, no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction in respect of any matter which the Federal Government or an officer apported under this Act is empowered under this Act to determine, and no junction, process or order shall be granted or issued by any Court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under this Analyzing Section 14 ibid, it is unambiguous that the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts have been barred with respect to any matter... which an officer appointed under the Act is empowered to determine: such jurisdiction is also ousted to grant and issue a junction, process or order MN respect of any action taken or to be taken by such officer in exercise of any power conferred by or under the Act, Briefly the facts to decide the petition are that the pet’t,oner joined F.].A. as Head Constable on 21.9 19*5 Annuity/h Inhale !AME position at Jinnah International 18 ? ?Nor w’ Wh6n h® Was placed under suspension on 30 3 poor,and T S6rVed with chase-sheet dates «nhm2« ° w along,th statement of allegations. Answer: The parties in case 2011 PLD 17 were: MUHAMMAD ANAYAT KHAN PETITIONER VERSUS ADDITIONAL DISTRICT JUDGE, POONCH, RAWALAKOT AJ&K AND ANOTHER— RESPONDENTS. This case was heard in HIGH COURT (AJ K).

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 2011 PLD 17.
Answer: GHULAM MUSTAFA MUGHAL, C J. ---Through this petition filed under section 44 of the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act, 1974 judgment and order passed by Additional District Judge, Pooch, respondent No.1 harm, on 15-52010 has been challenged for having been passed without lawful authority. Brief facts of the case are that respondent No.2, harm, rented out his shops situated at Supply Bazaar Rawalakot in 1985-86 to the petitioner herein, who filed an application under section of the AJ&K Rent Restriction Act, 1986 before the Rent Controller, Rawalakot on 29-4-2000 for determination of fair rent of the shops. After 3 weeks respondent No.2 herein, also filed an application in the same Court for ejectment of the petitioner from the said shops on the ground that respondent No. herein, without prior consent of the petitioner has sublet the shops and the same are required to him for his personal use. After receiving objections from the parties, the applications were consolidated and issues were framed. The parties were allowed an opportunity for leading evidence in support of their respective petitions. At the conclusion of the proceedings, the learned Senior Civil Judge/Rent Controller, Ravbialakot vide his judgment and order dated 28-10-2009 accepted the application for ejectment and disposed of the other application. An appeal was filed before the Appellate Authority, which, was dismissed Vide judgment dated 15-5- 2010. The order passed by the Appellate Authority has been challenged on the ground that respondent No. herein, has not been designated as Appellate Authority under the AJ&K Rent Restriction Act, 1986, hence, has no jurisdiction to hear and determine the appeals against the judgments of the Rent Controller, thus, the order passed by him in the mutant case is without jurisdictional competence and is a nullity in the eye of law. It was further alleged that respondent No. has earlier expressed himself while deciding an application for interim relief on 25-8-2006, therefore, by deciding this appeal he has acted as Judge in his own cause hence, the judgment is violative of the principle of natural justice. It is further stated that the question of default has not been attended by respondent No.1 in light of the record and the evidence has also not been appreciated properly and the conclusion drawn from the evidence is erroneous, illegal and violative of the settled principle of law. Respondent No.1 has been proceeded ex parte whereas respondent No.2 in his comments/written statement has refuted the stand taken in the petition and pleaded that the petitioner is defaulter since, 2004 and has also sublet the shops without prior consent of the respondent, hence, the Rent Controller as well as the Additional District Judge has rightly disposed of the controversy on the basis of the evidence brought on the record. It is further alleged that both the orders are based on evidence which was properly appreciated, hence, the decision is immune from interference in writ jurisdiction. Barrister Humayun Nawab Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner inter alia contended that the application for ejectment filed on behalf of respondent No.2 herein, was male FIDE because the same has been filed after 3 weeks of filing the application by the petitioner harm, for determination of the wait rent under section of the AJ&K Rent Restriction Act, 1986. He argued that the order passed by the Rent Controller as well as the Appellate Authority is illegal because neither the Rent Controller nor the Appellate Authority has disposed of the application for determination of the fair rent. He further argued that the judgment passed by the Additional District Judge is coral non juice because he was not designated as appellate Authority under the provisions contained in the AJ&K. Rent Restriction Act, 1986. The learned Advocate submitted that even otherwise, the learned Additional District Judge cannot act as Judge in his own cause because earlier he has disposed of an application regarding the term relief vide his order dated 25-8- 2006, therefore, he cannot hear the appeal. The learned Advocate contended that even the respondent has not proved that the shops were required to him for establishing his own business rather he wants to rent out the same to some other person. In support of his submission the learned Advocate placed reliance on PLD 1965 SC 459, PLD 1983 SC (AJ&K) 204 and 1997. CLC 1830. Mr. Muhammad Han if Min has, the learned Advocate for the respondents contended that the Rent Controller as well as the Appellate. Authority is a Special Tribunal constituted and appointed under the special law and its findings are based on evidence, which cannot be disturbed in writ jurisdiction. He further contended that no misreading or non -reading of evidence has been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, therefore, the petition cannot be entertained for appraisal or reappraisal of the question of facts. He argued that the appeal was made over to the Additional District Judge, who is designated Authority by virtue of the provisions contained in the AJ&K Rent Restriction Act, 1986 and the petitioner has appeared before the said authority without any objection and protest and after its decision against him, he cannot take an inconsistent position. The learned Advocate further contended that the authorities referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner have no relevancy so far the facts and legal position of the case m hand is concerned. The learned Advocate submitted that a special remedy is provided by the AJ&K Rent Restriction Act, 1986 and the petitioner is litigating from 29-4-2006. He argued that in an earlier round of litigation the matter was disposed of on appeal of the petitioner herein, by the same Additional District Judge, hence, after receiving benefit from the Omni he cannot blow both, hot and cold in the same threat. So far as the contention of Barrister Human Nawab Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner that Additional District Judge was not vested with the authority to Harland dispose of the appeal against the order passed by the Rent Controller is concerned the same is devoid of any force and the authority relied upon by him m this regard is also not applicable. Under section 15(1) of the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959 (Ordinance, VI of 1959) the Government has to confer the power of Appellate Authority by a notification on any District Judge for the purpose of that Ordinance, therefore, without any formal notification or designation of the Appellate Authority the District Judge was rightly held incompetent to hear the appeals as a principal Civil Court of the District. In case in hand, section 18 of the AJ&K Rent Restriction Act, 1986 is attracted which reads as under: "Appeal--(I) Any party aggrieved by an order of the Controller finally disposing of an application made under this Act may within thirty days of the date of such order, prefer an appeal in writing to the District Judge having jurisdiction over the area where the building or rented land m relation to which the order is passed, is situated: Provided that no appeal shall lie against an order made by a Controller under subsection (6) of S.14 determine approximately the amount of rent due or the rate of rent and directing the tenant to deposit all the rent due: Provided further that no appeal shall be from a interlocutory order passed by the Controller. (2) On such appeal being preferred, the District Judge may hear it himself or refer it for disposal to an Additional District Judge having jurisdiction over the area where the building or rented land in relation to which the order is passed, is situated. (3) The District Judge may recall an appeal made over by him to an Additional District Judge and either hear it himself or refer it for disposal of another Additional District Judge having jurisdiction as provided in subsection Section 18 reproduced hereinabove, provides a complete scheme for hearing and disposal of appeals by conferring powers on the District Judges and Additional District Judges, therefore; no notification in this regard is required. The Act itself has appointed District Judges as Appellate Authority having jurisdiction over the area where building or rented property relation to which the order is passed is situated. Under subsection (2) reproduced hereinabove, the'appeal can be heard toy the District Judge himself, or he can refer it for disposal to an Additional District Judge. The only embargo is that the Additional District Judge to whom appeal is entrusted should have jurisdiction over the subject - matter of dispute 1e. building or rented land should be situated in its respective jurisdiction and the appeal should have been entrusted to such Additional District Judge. This provision is enacted MN IME with section 24 of the C.P.C, which empowers the District Judge to make over any suit and case and recall the same for harem and disposal of the same by himself and again refer the same for disposal to any other Court of competent jurisdiction. In this case, as is evident from the order under challenge, the appeal was filed before the learned District Judge who made over the same to the learned Additional District Judge for disposal. The other authority relied upon by Barrister Humayun Nawab Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner is also not attracted in the present case. In that case the revisional jurisdiction was exercised by this Court against an order passed by the Rent Controller. The apex Court observed that as the Rent Controller as well as the Appellate Authority is special forum, created under the Rent Restriction Act and the Civil Procedure Code is not applicable to the proceedings before the Rent Controller, therefore, High Court was not vested with supervisory or revisional jurisdiction to enter tam the revision or revise the judgment/order passed by the Rent Controller or an Appellate Authority. In Khalid RAAF Mr's case [1997 CLC 1830] the apex Court observed that fan order of Special Tribunal or forum is passed on no evidence, or it suffers from a patent mistake or the order has not been passed keeping in view the relevant provisions of law, that is open to review in constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court. It was further observed that a bare statement of the landlord to the effect that he needed shops for running his own business did not prove the requirements of law. Analyst Khan and granted the application of Vardar M. Altar} respondent No.2 herein, has not been pleaded in IME of the respondents. In a case titled. Lt. (R) Muhammad Shabbir and 6 other's case [2003 YLR 346] the petition was dismissed on the ground that the SDM, who made the original report regarding the shifting of the School after visiting the spot MN pursuance Of which Government notifications issued, was not imp leaded in line of the respondents. A further reference can be made to Mira Law Hussein v. Custodian and others (1992 SCR 214), Muhammad Ashraf v. Azad Government and others (PLD 1985 SC (AJK) 102) and Muhammad Gresham Khan v. Chairman Inspection Team and others 1990 SC 1355(sic). In view of above, finding no substance, this petition is dismissed. Petition dismissed.

Question: Provide the full judgment for case 2011 PLD 296.
Answer: MIAN SAQIB NISAR, J.--The present appeal has its genesis in a suit for the specific performance filed by the appellant/plaintiff originally against Muhammad Din seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell dated 17-2-1986, whereby the latter statedly agreed to sell the suit property to him. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiff got imp leaded respondents Nos.2 to 9 as the defendants, being the subsequent vendees of the suit land vide nutation dated 24-8-1987. The defendants, so arrayed in their written statement, set out the defense under section 27(b) of Specific Relief Act 1877, BMG the bona fide purchasers of the land; however the original defendant as had denied the execution of the agreement to sell and parties were also discordant about the description of the property; therefore, inter alia three important issues 1.e. (1) about the execution of the agreement, (iv) qua the description of the property and (vi) and about the bona fide purchase of the said defendants were framed. The learned trial Court after recording of the evidence, by returning its finding in favor of the plaintiff on Issue No.(1) and deciding the other two issues against the defendants, passed the decree for specific performance dated 12-10- 2000. The said judgment and decree was challenged by the subsequent vendees, in appeal which was accepted by reversing the findings only to their extent being the bona fide purchasers, while the finding of the trial Court on other two issues were affirmed, with the result that the suit was dismissed through the judgment and decree dated 12-10-2000. The appellant challenged this verdict in a civil revision before the Lahore High Court, but without any success. It has been held: - "the learned appellate court Lias rightly held that after the testimony of die respondents witnesses asserting that they were unaware of the existence of the aforesaid agreement, the onus shifted on to the petitioner/plaintiff to prove through affirmative evidence that the respondents/defendants had knowledge of the said agreement and as such, they were not bona fide purchaser. There can be no cavil with this well-established Legal principle. (4) I have myself gone through, the evidence of the witnesses produced by the petitioner/plaintiff and find that there is no evidence to establish that the respondent/defendants had notice of the agreement Ex.P.1. in the circumstances, the impugned appellate decree is not open to exception. Leave in this case was granted on 1-1-2009 to consider if the view set out by the appellate and revisional Courts is in consonance with the law laid down by this Court regarding the above proposition. 3. Learned counsel for the appellant has relied upon the following judgments: Raoul Baths Nacli v. Syed Raoul Baths Shah (2010 SCMR 988), M. Din v. MST. Sabina Bibi (2003 SCMR 956), MST. Surra ya Begum and others v. MST. Rubati Begum (1992 SCMR 652), M. Ashraf v. Ali Haman (1992 SCMR 1942), MST. There-ul-Nisa v: Malik M. Ishfaque (PLD 1972 SC 25), Heidi Abdul Regina and others v. Noa Ahmed and others (PLD 1974- Baghdad-UL-Jadid 25), M. Shall v. M. Salwar (1997 CLC 1231), Kathiawar v. Shah Muhammad (1984 CLC 22), M. Yousaf Issue v. Abdul Majid Khan and others (1984 CLC 243) and Malik M. Issue and others v. Mira Adam Ali Beige and others (PLD 1969 L,ah 762) to argue that the subsequent Vendée asserting to be a bona fide purchaser having no knowledge/notice of the prior agreement to sell, is required to lead affirmative evidence to that effect; such essential evidence according to learned counsel however is conspicuously missing in this case, therefore the view of the two Courts holding that the respondents are protected by the said equitable rule is against the settled law. 4. Heard. The principles regarding the burden (onus) of proof, particularly in the civil litigation are elucidated by the provisions of Articles 117 to 120 of the QAnon-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, which for the facility of reference are reproduced as below:- "117. Burden of proof-(1) Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or ability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. (2) When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person. 118. On whom burden of proof lies.--The burden of proofing a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail info evidence at all were given on either side. 119. Burden of proof as to particular fact.--The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on that person who wishes the Court to believe in its existence, unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on any particular person. 120. Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible.--The burden of proving any fact necessary to be proved in order to enable any person to give evidence of any other fact is on the person who wishes to give such evidence. From the analysis and collective reading of the above provisions, it is manifest and unambiguously clear that in a dispute between the parties in a civil litigation, the resolution whereof is dependant upon the existence of certain facts which are not self-evident, and a party to the is wants the Court to believe about the existence of those and seek verdict in his favor, the onus to prove shall be on the shoulder of such litigant who asserts the existence of the fact. In the cases pertain and relating to the protection under section 27(b) of the Specific Reef Act, 1877, undoubtedly, it is the subsequent Vendée who asserts and avows in the defense that his case falls within the purview and parameter of the noted section Le. he is a transferee for value; the money (consideration) has been paid in good faith; and that he had no notice of the original (earlier) contract between the plaintiff and the vendor. In other words that lie is a Bona tide purchaser without notice. Obviously the existence of the facts aforementioned and the ascertainment thereof is an issue between the parties which requires resolution from the Court. It is therefore in such like cases by applying the rules regarding burden of proof as emerging from the noted Articles, especially 117 and 118, the initial onus to prove the same is on the shoulder of the subsequent Vendée. It may be pertinent to post out that in civil disputes the onus to prove a fact however does not remain constant or stagnant, thus once the initial onus on a proposition of fact has been discharged by the side upon whom TT was originally placed, it would shift over to the other party for the rebuttal thereof or for the proof otherwise. 5. Be that as it may, the subsequent Vendée thus has to discharge the initial onus as follows: (1) that he acquired the property for due consideration and thus is a transferee for value, meaning thereby that his purchase is for the price paid to the vendor and not otherwise. (2) there was no dishonesty of purpose or tainted intention to enter MTO the transaction which shall settle that he acted in good faith or with bona fide; (3) he had no knowledge or the notice of the original sale agreement between the plaintiff and the vendor at the time of his transaction with the latter. From the above it is depicted that the section merely enacts the English equitable rule which allows later legal title to prevail over an equitable interest in case of bona fide purchaser for value without notice (emphases supplied). And this principle has to be kept in view by the Courts while analyzing and appreciating the evidence on the record for the discharge of the requisite burden. 6. In the afore-noted context, it is thus required that a subsequent Vendée should adduce in evidence his sale instrument or the mutation of his transaction, if not otherwise on the record having been brought by the plaintiff himself or any other proof in this connection such as the receipt of payment made to the vendor or the bank record etc. or should lead credible, oral evidence in this behalf} these are some conceivable modes of proving the transfer for value and shall be a sufficient discharge of onus in this respect in ordinary cases. If however, a specific attack has been made in the plant or the replication by the plaintiff that the subsequent transaction is without consideration, or the value given is colorable, understated, underpaid and illusionary, it becomes the ( bounden duty of the subsequent transferee to establish through positive evidence that adequate price was paid, because this fac tum shall also have a close nexus to the good faith and the bona fides of the said transferee as well; when it is so done, the onus shall switch over to the plaintiff to prove otherwise. 7. The second ingredient "good faith" is the term which reflects the state of mind and according to section 3(20) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 "a thing shall be deemed to. be done in 'good faith' where it is in fact done honestly, whether it is done negligently or not". While interpreting this, it was held in Nanny Mai v. Rani Chandler (AIR 1931 All 277 (FB)) that good faith as defined above is equivalent to honesty of dealing arid does not entail upon the purchaser the necessity of searching the registry, even assuming that there were facts indicative of negligence in investigating title, that by itself was not predicative of alack of Bona tides. Therefore, the second condition shall stand settled if the subsequent Vendée has acted as a man of ordinary prudence m retaking inquiries expected from a purchaser who wants to acquire a good title for the price/value he is pay mg. This may include the checking of the Revenue Record or obtain the copies thereof to verify about the title of the vendor OT any third party in right, east or charge over the property or any endorsement in such record about any pending litigation or an injunctive order etc.; this may be a good and adequate exercise of investigative process, in case of rural/agriculture property. And for the same purpose, regarding urban property, the Excise and Taxation record may be examined coupled with the verification and obtaining the original documents of title from the vendor, if those are available. However, the subsequent Vendée is not obliged to run from the pillar to post in conducting rowing and fish mg inquiries, to ascertain if a third party has any merest etc. In the property which otherwise is visibly lacking. But if there exist some overt, prominent and conspicuous indicators about the third party interest, which are so patently noticeable and manifest that those could not and should not be missed aid ignored by a purchaser, such as the possession not with the vendor but someone else, who is approached or its nature investigated would lead to discover such interest, the purchaser is obliged to probe about it, otherwise he may not be able to take resort of the noted equitable rule. If therefore a subsequent Vendée has taken due care in the above manner and there are no indicators to put him to a notice of third party merest, he shall be said to have acted in good faith, thus satisfying the second condition of the rule. 8. The last and the utmost important ingredient of section 27(b) is the lack of knowledge or the notice of the subsequent Vendée about the original contract between the plaintiff of the case and the vendor. This undoubtedly is the negative fact which cannot be conclusively proved in positive terms as it is conceivable that such fact could be established by affirmative means. To illustrate the point; if the marriage between the parties is an admitted fact but due to the subsequent assertion of the husband that it has been terminated on account of divorce pronounced by him; the wife who refutes it and in order to safeguard her marital status and the nights flowing therefrom is constrained to institute a suit for activation, in which the man sets out (obviously) the defense of divorce; the factual proposition with reference to the noted facts which would emerge for the resolution and determination of the Court would be whether the plaintiffs is still the wife of the defendant? and/or whether the defendant has divorced the plaintiff? Viewing it from any angle the fact'that the marriage on account of divorce by the husband stands dissolved is a negative fact, for the wife to prove. Another example may further elucidate the post, in an ejectment petition, the landlord seeks the eviction of his tenant on the ground of default in the payment of rent, which fact is denied by the tenant, now it shall not be possible for the landlord to prove in the positive term that the rent has not been paid, which again is a negative proof of fact, thus the landlord shall be said to have discharged the initial burden of proof by making statement on oath about the lack of payment of rent, which shall be subject to cross-examination by the other side, thereafter, the onus shall be on the tenant to prove in positive terms that the rent Lias been paid. The above example shall also be true with reference to the first illustration, because if a wife makes a statement on oath about the subsistence of marriage between the parties and deny the divorce, she shall be considered in law to have discharged the initial onus, which shall switch over to the husband for the proof otherwise, by positive evidence. Because such a negative fact the law of evidence universally recognizes is not capable of proof positively. 9. Considering the above rule in context with the proposition in hand in Leslie Singh v. Dark Path and others (AIR 1929 Lahore 249) it has been held: - "The onus of proving that the subsequent purchaser had no notice of a prior claim lies on such purchaser; and the onus of such a negative issue is ordinarily discharged by a denial and by a negative evidence." In MST. There-ul-Nisa and 6 others v. Malik Muhammad Issue and 2 others (PLD 1972 SC 25) this Court ordained: "Under section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act negative is to be proved by the subsequent transferee. If he appears in Court and states on oath that lie had no knowledge of the transfer that ( would be quite sufficient to discharge the burden and the onus will, then shift to the plaintiff to prove that the subsequent transferee had the notice of the original contract". In MST. Surra ya Begum and others v. MST. Cuban Begum and others (1992 SCMR 652) while dilating on the proposition this Court laid down the law:- "Since in civil suits an issue is to be decided by preponderance of evidence, the mutual burden would be on the plaintiff to prove his prior contract, which is discharged, the burden of proving the subsequent bona fide transfer for value without notice would be on the party alleging TT. Very little evidence and MN certain circumstances a mere denial regarding want of knowledge of the earlier contract would discharge this burden and shift the onus on the plaintiff to prove that the subsequent transferee had the notice of the earlier contract." In the light of the noted authoritative pronouncements, it can be safely concluded that though the initial onus is on the subsequent Vendée, however, it is light one, and once it is discharged by abiding by the criteria set out hereinabove, it shall be the burden and duty of the plaintiff to prove positively that the subsequent Vendée had the notice of his sale agreement; besides, the subsequent transaction is without the passing of the due consideration; it is a colorable or a fraudulent transaction entered into with dishonesty of purpose by the vendor and the subsequent Vendée in order to cause prejudice, his rights under the sale agreement. This in our view to an extent should settle the law regarding the rule providing protection to bona fide purchaser for value without notice and the standards of proof thereof. 10. Now, it-is expedient to evaluate if the subsequent vendees in the present case have discharged their mitral burden of the issue on the criteria as has been set out above, suffice it to say that the mutation of subsequent sale has been produced by them in evidence; Ghulam Hussain, one of the vendees, appeared and deposed about the quantum and payment of the price, but he was not cross-examined; the appellant while appearing as P.W.8 in his cross- examination has also admitted that the suit property was purchased by the said respondents for a price of Rs.3,50,000 which was prior to the institution of the suit; moreover, a suggestion was given to Ghulam Hussain MN the cross-examination that the subsequent vendees were informed by the relatives of the plaintiff about the agreement to sell, which he denied, but in rebuttal'in such evidence was led to prove the passing of such an information. D.W:1, one of the vendees, appeared acid testified about the lack of knowledge of the prior agreement, no cross-examination was again conducted on his, this deposition; the said witness stated that the copies of the Revenue Record were procured by subsequent transferee, there is no cross-examination to refute the above; it is specifically mentioned by the witnesses that the plaintiff or any other third person was not in possession of the suit land and the subsequent vendees pursuant to their sale got the possession of the property from the vendor, this too was not subject to cross-examination. This all brings the case within the realm of the principle that if a material fact Lias been deposed in the examination in-chief, and it is not subjected to the cross-examination, it shall be deemed to have been admitted. The elements of overt indicators are also conspicuously missing in the case; there is no corporation of the appellant's agreement in the Revenue Record. Besides, the most vital and striking aspect of the case is that the plaintiff in rebuttal to the relevant issue after the evidence was led by the respondents who had discharged their mitral onus has led no evidence (emphasis supplied) at all to prove that the respondents lacked in the payment, their transfer is male FIDE and is meant to effect the (plaintiffs) equitable interest under the agreement. And above all that they (subsequent vendees) had the notice of their sale agreement. This omission is a very fatal lapse on their part. Thus, the views set out by the appellate Court and the High Court that the nights of the respondents are protected under section 27(b) of the Act (ibid) are unexceptionable. This appeal, therefore, has, no merits and is hereby dismissed. Appeal dismissed.

The principles regarding the burden (onus) of proof, particularly in the civil litigation are elucidated by the provisions of Articles 117 to 120 of the QAnon-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, which for the facility of reference are reproduced as below:- "117. Burden of proof-(1) Whoever desires any Court to give judgment as to any legal right or ability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist. (2) When a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person. 118. On whom burden of proof lies.--The burden of proofing a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail info evidence at all were given on either side. 119. Burden of proof as to particular fact.--The burden of proof as to any particular fact lies on that person who wishes the Court to believe in its existence, unless it is provided by any law that the proof of that fact shall lie on any particular person. 120. Burden of proving fact to be proved to make evidence admissible.--The burden of proving any fact necessary to be proved in order to enable any person to give evidence of any other fact is on the person who wishes to give such evidence. From the analysis and collective reading of the above provisions, it is manifest and unambiguously clear that in a dispute between the parties in a civil litigation, the resolution whereof is dependant upon the existence of certain facts which are not self-evident, and a party to the is wants the Court to believe about the existence of those and seek verdict in his favor, the onus to prove shall be on the shoulder of such litigant who asserts the existence of the fact. In the cases pertain and relating to the protection under section 27(b) of the Specific Reef Act, 1877, undoubtedly, it is the subsequent Vendée who asserts and avows

It is therefore in such like cases by applying the rules regarding burden of proof as emerging from the noted Articles, especially 117 and 118, the initial onus to prove the same is on the shoulder of the subsequent Vendée. It may be pertinent to post out that in civil disputes the onus to prove a fact however does not remain constant or stagnant, thus once the initial onus on a proposition of fact has been discharged by the side upon whom TT was originally placed, it would shift over to the other party for the rebuttal thereof or for the proof otherwise. 5. Be that as it may, the subsequent Vendée thus has to discharge the initial onus as follows: (1) that he acquired the property for due consideration and thus is a transferee for value, meaning thereby that his purchase is for the price paid to the vendor and not otherwise. (2) there was no dishonesty of purpose or tainted intention to enter MTO the transaction which shall settle that he acted in good faith or with bona fide; (3) he had no knowledge or the notice of the original sale agreement between the plaintiff and the vendor at the time of his transaction with the latter. Question: Provide the full judgment for case 2011 PLD 126.
Answer: MIAN SAQIB NISAR, J.--The suit for declaration etc. filed by the respondent-plaintiff against the appellant-defendant, after the contest and trial was decreed by the learned Civil Judge, Swabia vide judgment and decree dated 3-7-2002 holding that the house in dispute has been validly transferred to the respondent by the Evacuee Department, and it has not been established by the appellant to be attached to any charitable/religious trust etc. to form part of an evacuee trust property. However, on the crucial objection, raised by the appellant which had culminated into Issue No.2 it was ostensibly found by the trial Court having no jurisdiction in the matter, yet strangely the suit as mentioned earlier was decreed. The appeal of the appellant, which was filed through Assistant Administrator, Evacuee Trust Property, Peshawar, was dismissed by the Additional District Judge on 5-3-2003 while upholding the decision of the trial Court as a whole, and for an additional reason that the appeal was instituted by an officer, who was not competent to do so: these judgments and decrees have been sustained by the Peshawar High Court through its judgment dated 19- 12-2003. Leave to appeal was granted in this case on 26-1-2006 in the following terms:- "Contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner is that the suit filed by the respondent/plaintiff was barred by law as such civil Court has no jurisdiction to grant the declaration prayed for in view of the bar contained in section 14 of PTFE Evacuee Trust Properties (Management and Disposal) Act (XIII of 1975) and such plea was raised before the trial Court and as such issue was also framed and finding of the suit on Issue No. was to the effect that the Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit, yet the suit was decreed and declaration was granted declaring the suit property to be non-evacuee." 2. The brief facts germane for the disposal of the present appeal, are: the house in question measuring about four Marley, situated in village Aida (Swabia) was transferred to the respondent by the Assistant Settlement Commissioner (Lands), Marian through PTO dated 6-10-1967 on the payment of Rs.1010. On the strength of the above, the respondent on 13-6-1996 brought the suit seeking declaration about his exclusive ownership of the house and asserting that the appellant has no right or concern thereto, with an additional claim of permanent injunctive relief that the appellant should not meddle with his ownership and possessory rights qua the suit property. The appellant in its written WW. statement took up the specific objection regarding the jurisdiction of the civil Court to entertain and try the suit, which objection obviously was in terms of section 14 read with other enable provisions of Evacuee Trust Properties (Management and Disposal) Act (XIII), 1975 (hereafter referred to as the Act). It may be percent to mention here that in the first stance the learned Civil Judge seized of the case vide order dated 3-4-2000, rejected the plaint of the respondent under Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C. holding that it has no jurisdiction to hear the matter, which (jurisdiction) is barred by law. The respondent preferred an appeal which was allowed and by setting aside the order impugned their, the case was remanded with the direction that such objection should form MTO an issue and should be decided along with other issues involved in the matter. Upon trial, the learned Civil Judge on the issue of jurisdiction has come to the conclusion "In the light of above discussion, it is held that this Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the instant suit. This issue is therefore decided in positive" emphasis supplied). It may be relevant to mention here that from the reproduced part of the findings of the trial Court and of the leave granting order, an impression can be gathered that the Civil Judge seized of the matter decided the issue of jurisdiction against the respondent and yet decreed the suit. But upon reading of the specific wordings of Issue No.2 1e. "whether this Court has no jurisdiction to restrain (sic) the present suit?" Our view is otherwise, because the discussion on this issue by the trial Court especially the portion "the objection with respect to Bar of jurisdiction under section 14 of TTB, B(sic) Act, 1975 appears to have no force" leads us to form an option that the finding is that the Court has the jurisdiction. Be that as it may, the revisional Court (the High Court) having final say in the matter by relying upon the judgment of this Court reported as Evacuee Trust Property Board through Assistant Administrator, Evacuee Trust Property Board at Mirpur Khas v. Abdul Aziz Khan and 6 others (2000 SCMR 1371) particularly by quoting a portion therefrom i.e. "Since in law the disputed property had not been treated as evacuee trust property, therefore, the bar of jurisdiction cannot be pressed into service. For the ouster of Jurisdiction, the petitioner ought to have proved through cogent evidence that the disputed property was attached to a charitable trust and as such no suit was maintainable in respect thereof" Therefore, on the touchstone of the above and while examining the documentary evidence, produced by the appellant, the revisional Court came to the conclusion that from none of WW. such documents it is established if either the suit property was declared to be an evacuee trust property by the Chairman or was ever so treated; and/or even the said documents do not relate to the suit property. It is, therefore, on account of this that the decisions of the two Courts were upheld by dismissing the revision petition of the appellant. 3. Learned counsel for the appellant states that in terms of section 8 of the Act that it is the exclusive jurisdiction of the Chairman, Evacuee Trust Property Board to adjudge, decide and declare whether any property is an evacuee trust property or not; besides the validation of CERTAM transfers of the properties which are considered to be evacuee trust properties shall also be within the sole and exclusive empowerment of the Chairman and the jurisdiction of the civil Courts in relation to these powers/questions is expressly barred by the two noted provisions of law. Further by making reference to section 14 of the Act, it is submitted that there is an express bar for the exercise of the jurisdiction by the civil Court in respect of any action which an officer appointed under the Act is empowered to determine or to take or to be taken in exercise of any power conferred upon him by or under the Act. In support of his submissions, he has also relied upon the cases reported as Evacuee Trust Property Board and others v. Ahmed and others (2004 SCMR 440), Evacuee Trust Property Board and others v. MST. Sabina Bibi and others (2007 SCMR 262), Sugar Department through Chief Administrator Sugar, Punjab, Lahore v. Secretary, Ministry of Religious Zakat, Usher and Minorities Affairs, Government of Pakistan, Islamabad and 3 others (2009 SCMR 210) and Evacuee Trust Property Board v. Sheikh Abdul Attar and another (2009 SCMR 1223). Whereas, contrary to the above, learned counsel for the respondent, has relied upon 2000 SCMR 1371 (supra) the judgment on which reliance has been placed by the High Court. 4. Heard. From the above-mentioned provisions of the Act and the case-law cited, it is clear that for the actions/orders etc. mentioned in the section, an express bar has been placed upon the exercise of jurisdiction by the civil Courts. However, when the facts of the present case are examined in the light of the evidence brought on the record by the parties particularly the appellant, it has conspicuously emerged that no declaration under section 8 of the Act assigning the suit property a status of evacuee trust property has been made by the Chairman, Evacuee Trust Property Board. Likewise, the validity of the transfer made in favor of the respondent by the evacuee department through the PTO referred to above WW. has not been determined and adjudicated by the Chairman as required under section 10 of the Act. Obviously, in such a situation the specific bar contemplated by the noted two sections shall not be attracted. As regards, the general bar of section 14 is concerned, on the basis of which leave was granted by this Court, it (the section) reads as under: Bar of jurisdiction.-- Save as otherwise provided in this Act, no civil Court shall have jurisdiction in respect of any matter which the Federal Government or an officer appointed under this Act is empowered under this Act to determine, and no injunction, process or order shall be granted or issued by any Court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in exercise of any power conferred by or under this Act." Analyzing section 14 ibid, it is unambiguous that the jurisdiction of the civil Courts have been barred with respect to any matter. which an officer apported under the Act is empowered to determine: such jurisdiction is also ousted to grant and issue an injunction, process or order in respect of any action taken or to be taken by such officer in exercise of any power conferred by or under the Act. Undoubtedly, the Chairman of the Evacuee Trust Property Board is an officer within the contemplation of the section. Therefore, in order to settle the question about the ouster of jurisdiction it seems expedient to examine, what was the proposition evolved in the suit and whether such a question was determinable by the Chairman or not: In this respect, it is foundational to evaluate the clam of the respondent in his suit/plaint; on the perusal thereof it is vivid that the respondent is seeking a declaration that the suit property is his exclusive ownership and is not an evacuee trust property, consequently the appellant should be precluded from interfere MTO his ownership nights and apprentices thereto; the appellant in defense joined issue with the respondent on these factual aspects and claimed the suit property being an evacuee trust property, and it is on this account that the jurisdiction of the Court was challenged. Therefore, the key issue before the Court would be whether the property is an evacuee trust property or otherwise? Now when the provisions of section 8 of the Act are adverted to, it specially mentions "if a question arises whether an evacuee property is attached to a charitable, religious or educational trust, or not it shall be decided by the Chairman" meaning thereby that notwithstanding whether a declaration in terms of section 8 has been made or not by the Chairman, yet even if a question has arisen at any point of time about the status of the property it shall be the Chairman alone who under the Act shall be competent and empowered to determine and decide the question and the Court in view of the bar contained in Section 14 shall have no jurisdiction in the matter. 5. Whether the question of the above nature was/is involved in the matter is clear from the pleadings of the parties and from the findings of all the Courts below on Issue No.5 Le. whether the plaintiff is entitled to decree as prayed for? As the Courts while considering and appreciating the evidence of the parties on the record have come to the conclusion ( that the property is not established by the appellant to be attached to any charitable, religious trust etc. thus is not an evacuee trust property. This determination, in our considered view, was within the exclusive domain of the Chairman and the adjudication thereof by the Courts is an encroachment and circumvention on his empowerment. Therefore, the bar of section 14 ibid was duly attracted. 5A. In the light of the above, while allowing this appeal the judgments and decrees of all the Courts below are hereby set aside and the suit of the respondent its dismissed due to the lack of jurisdiction of the civil Court. Appeal allowed.

Answer: JUDGMENT C.M.A. NO. 6863 OF 2014 IN CIVILAPPEAL NO. 56 OF 2011, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 462-L OF 2009 AND CIVILAPPEAL NO.11-L OF 2013. Statutes CONTRACT ACT (IX OF 1872)-SS.
